author: Fowler
title: Task-Specific Layer-by-Layer Distillation to Enhance Language Model Compression
abstract: Compressing large-scale teacher models into smaller student models can be effectively achieved via layer-wise distillation, where the student replicates the teacher’s intermediate hidden states. Nevertheless, this approach faces difficulties because the reduced capacity of the student often leads to underfitting, and the teacher’s representations include extraneous information irrelevant to the target task. To overcome these issues, we introduce a task-specific layer-wise distillation technique that employs filters tailored to the target task. These filters selectively extract relevant knowledge from each layer’s teacher hidden representations to better align with the student’s features. By focusing on task-relevant information, our method narrows the discrepancy between teacher and student, thereby improving student model fitting on the task. The effectiveness of this approach is validated across continual pre-training and fine-tuning settings, where it attains consistent and notable gains compared to previous distillation methods.

author: Johnson
title: Addressing Gender Bias in Compressed Language Models through Counterfactual Role Inversion
abstract: The strong performance of language models in generating coherent sequences has been extended to environments with limited resources via model compression techniques like knowledge distillation. Despite their efficacy, these distilled models may retain or amplify biases present in a teacher model, such as spurious connections between gender identities and gender-neutral occupations. Unconstrained knowledge distillation processes risk perpetuating these biases in the student model. To tackle this, we introduce a method for producing a fairer student model during the knowledge distillation process. Our method implements two key alterations to the conventional distillation framework leveraging counterfactual role inversion: adjusting the teacher’s output probabilities and enriching the training dataset. Using distilled and subsequently fine-tuned GPT-2 models, we assess gender bias by measuring gender polarity in profession-related open-ended text generation, finding a significant decline in gender bias alongside only a slight degradation in model utility. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that reductions in gender polarity during text generation do not correspond to improvements in embedding fairness or fairness in downstream classification tasks.

author: Hill
title: A Deep Hierarchical Framework for Continuous Learning in Minecraft
abstract: We introduce a continuous learning framework capable of transferring and reusing knowledge across tasks while maintaining previously acquired information effectively. The transfer mechanism is based on acquiring reusable skills for solving tasks within Minecraft, a popular video game embodying a challenging high-dimensional lifelong learning scenario. These reusable skills, termed Deep Skill Networks in our approach, are integrated into a novel Hierarchical Deep Reinforcement Learning Network (H-DRLN) architecture through two methods: (1) a deep skill array and (2) skill distillation, a new variant of policy distillation (Rusu et al., 2015) designed specifically for skill acquisition. Skill distillation facilitates the H-DRLN to consolidate knowledge efficiently and thus supports scalability in lifelong learning by aggregating and compressing multiple reusable skills into a single distilled model. Compared to the standard Deep Q Network (Mnih et al., 2015), the H-DRLN demonstrates enhanced performance and reduced training sample requirements in various Minecraft sub-domains.

author: Walker
title: Meta Learning Framework for Adaptive Knowledge Distillation from BERT to Student Models
abstract: We propose a novel approach to knowledge distillation that integrates meta learning, contrasting the common practice of keeping the teacher model static during student training. Our method enables the teacher network to enhance its knowledge transfer capabilities by leveraging feedback derived from the student's distilled performance, effectively embodying a learning-to-teach paradigm. Additionally, we develop a pilot update strategy designed to better synchronize the meta-learner and inner-learner components in meta learning algorithms that prioritize refining the inner-learner. Through a series of tests across multiple benchmark datasets, our approach demonstrates substantial gains over conventional knowledge distillation techniques, exhibiting reduced sensitivity to student network size and hyperparameter variations, thereby supporting its applicability across varied tasks and architectures.

author: Doyle
title: A Knowledge Distillation Approach for Recommender Systems Combining Latent and Predictive Teacher Knowledge
abstract: Knowledge distillation, a compression approach that transfers information from a large teacher model to a smaller student model, has been adopted in recent recommender systems to reduce inference delay without sacrificing accuracy. Existing leading techniques predominantly concentrate on aligning the student's outputs with the teacher's predictions, which limits access to the complete knowledge contained within the teacher model. To address this issue, we introduce a knowledge distillation framework for recommender systems that facilitates the student in acquiring both the implicit information embedded in the teacher and its predictive outputs. This framework consists of two components: (1) Distillation Experts, designed to convey the teacher's underlying knowledge through a set of specialized modules alongside an innovative expert selection mechanism tailored for transferring substantial knowledge to a resource-constrained student; and (2) Relaxed Ranking Distillation, which captures the nuanced relative orderings present in the teacher's predictions to inform student training. Comprehensive evaluations demonstrate that the proposed method surpasses current top-performing techniques and achieves inference speeds that are faster than the original teacher model while delivering similar or improved recommendation accuracy.

author: Rhodes
title: Continual Knowledge Transfer for Language Learning Across Tasks
abstract: Achieving lifelong language learning (LLL) on a sequence of diverse tasks without suffering performance drops relative to multi-task baselines remains challenging. To tackle this problem, we introduce a straightforward yet effective technique applicable to current LLL frameworks to reduce such performance decline. Concretely, for each new task during LLL training, a teacher model is first trained to acquire the new task's knowledge, which is subsequently distilled into the LLL model. This process enables the LLL model to integrate the novel task more effectively while preserving knowledge from preceding tasks. Empirical results demonstrate that the proposed method consistently enhances existing top-performing models and significantly diminishes degradation compared to multi-task training across LLL scenarios, covering both sequence generation and text classification tasks.

author: Mcclain
title: Transferring Internal Representations for Knowledge Distillation
abstract: Commonly, knowledge distillation involves training a compact student model to replicate the behavior of a larger teacher model. This is achieved by leveraging the teacher's output probabilities as soft labels during student optimization to compress its knowledge. Nevertheless, for very large teacher networks, there is no certainty that the student inherits the teacher's internal representations; even if the student's output probabilities align well with the teacher's, its intermediate features can differ substantially. Such discrepancies in internal representations may compromise the student's intended generalization that knowledge distillation seeks to transmit. Here, we introduce a method to transfer the internal representations from a sizable model like BERT into a streamlined counterpart. We define two approaches for internal representation distillation along with several algorithmic implementations to realize this process. Utilizing benchmarks from GLUE, our experiments demonstrate that incorporating distillation from internal layers consistently outperforms approaches relying solely on output probability distillation.

author: Miller
title: Enhancing Spoken Question Answering Accuracy through Knowledge Distillation
abstract: Spoken question answering (SQA) challenges machines to accurately interpret complex audio documents. The effectiveness of QA systems heavily depends on automatic speech recognition (ASR), yet recent studies indicate that ASR transcripts are often noisy, significantly hindering machine comprehension in SQA. To mitigate this problem, we propose a new knowledge distillation framework. Our approach involves a targeted training regimen that distills knowledge from both spoken inputs and their corresponding text versions. By leveraging the language model's guidance during distillation, we improve the student model’s accuracy by minimizing discrepancies between automatic and manual speech transcriptions. Experimental results show that the proposed method achieves superior performance compared to multiple leading language models on the Spoken-SQuAD benchmark.

author: Henderson
title: Ensemble Compression through Adversarial Distillation of Multiple Models
abstract: Deep neural networks that combine predictions from several base models frequently outperform individual networks. However, deploying such ensembles in scenarios with large test datasets, like ImageNet, is hindered by their substantial storage demands and slow test-time computation. This study introduces a technique to condense extensive and intricate ensembles composed of multiple trained DNNs into a singular network by distilling and transferring knowledge from several teacher networks into one student DNN. To capture the varied expertise from these teacher models, an adversarial learning framework is developed, where a block-wise training loss is employed to steer the student network to approximate the teacher feature representations, while concurrently a discriminator is trained to differentiate features originating from teachers versus the student. The resulting ensemble compression method delivers three key benefits: (1) the student network, trained with discriminators to distill knowledge, surpasses the optimization level of the initial base models; (2) inference acceleration is achieved through the single forward evaluation of the student, whose accuracy exceeds that of standard ensembles aggregating multiple original networks; (3) the student architecture can effectively absorb distilled knowledge from teacher models with heterogeneous architectures. Extensive empirical validation on CIFAR-10/100, SVHN, and ImageNet datasets confirms the approach’s effectiveness. Specifically, on ImageNet, the ResNet-50 based distilled student obtains top-1 and top-5 validation errors of 21.79% and 5.99%, improving by 2.06% and 1.14% respectively over the base network. Code and pretrained weights can be found at https://github.com/AaronHeee/MEAL

author: Robinson
title: Developing Teachers Optimized for Student Models in Knowledge Distillation
abstract: This work introduces a knowledge distillation technique designed to enhance the delivery of dark knowledge from teachers to students. Unlike typical approaches focusing on training student networks using fixed pretrained teachers, our method concentrates on constructing teacher models specifically tailored to be compatible with student networks, thereby better facilitating knowledge transfer. Put differently, during the teacher training phase, our framework simultaneously optimizes a set of student branches to produce representations that are more accommodating for student learning. Because the principal objective is refining teacher training, and the knowledge distillation process following this is direct, this strategy can be integrated into a wide range of existing knowledge distillation frameworks, enhancing both the accuracy and training speed of various student architectures. Empirical results show that our algorithm attains superior accuracy within multiple established knowledge distillation setups involving diverse combinations of teacher and student structures, including scenarios where the architectures differ significantly and no prior information about the student models is accessible during teacher training.

author: Wagner
title: Knowledge Distillation from a Model’s Own Outputs for NLP Applications
abstract: Deep learning models have become dominant in natural language processing (NLP), achieving exceptional results across numerous tasks, occasionally surpassing human benchmarks. This success is largely attributed to their capability to encode knowledge effectively. Although various approaches aim to enhance representation learning, leveraging knowledge distillation from pretrained networks demonstrates that soft target probabilities carry additional useful information for training other neural architectures. Here, we introduce a novel distillation technique termed self-knowledge distillation, which utilizes the training model’s own soft target probabilities, extracting multimodal cues from the word embedding layer immediately preceding softmax. Due to computational constraints, our approach employs an approximation of these soft targets. We evaluated this method on two essential NLP problems—language modeling and neural machine translation—finding that our approach yields performance gains in both domains.

author: Johnson
title: Theoretical Analysis of Knowledge Distillation in Wide Networks: Generalization Limits, Efficiency, and Teacher Imperfections
abstract: Training a student model by leveraging the softened outputs produced by a teacher network constitutes the knowledge distillation paradigm, widely applied for compressing models and transferring expertise. Despite its empirical success, a rigorous theoretical foundation for knowledge distillation remains underdeveloped. Recent advances utilizing neural tangent kernel theory allow a wide neural network to be closely approximated by a linear predictor defined by the network's randomly initialized features. Our study offers a theoretical treatment of knowledge distillation applied to such wide architectures. We first establish an upper bound on the transfer risk associated with the linearized network model. Subsequently, we introduce a novel concept termed data inefficiency that quantifies the intrinsic training challenge of a task. Utilizing this, our results indicate that when the teacher network is flawless, emphasizing a large proportion of the teacher's softened outputs during distillation can lead to improved outcomes. Lastly, in scenarios involving teachers that make imperfect predictions, incorporating hard labels aids in correcting the teacher's errors, thereby supporting the common practice of combining hard and soft label supervision.

author: Gonzalez
title: Emphasizing Each Training Phase: Knowledge Distillation Through Joint Instruction
abstract: Deploying deep neural networks on devices with limited resources is hindered by their high demands for storage and computation. Knowledge distillation addresses this by training a smaller student network via knowledge transfer from a larger, pre-trained teacher model. Yet, many current distillation approaches overlook the informative content present during the intermediate training stages alongside the final outcomes. This study introduces a strategy that applies dual specialized teachers within a collaborative teaching knowledge distillation framework. One teacher, trained from initialization (termed the scratch teacher), provides incremental guidance by sharing its evolving outputs, thereby steering the student progressively towards the final high-accuracy logits. The other teacher, pretrained (termed the expert teacher), encourages the student to concentrate on key regions valuable for the target task. Integrating knowledge from these two distinctive teachers notably enhances the student network's distillation performance. Experimental evaluation across CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, SVHN, and Tiny ImageNet datasets demonstrates that the proposed method is effective and attains top-tier results.

author: Santos
title: Channel-Wise Attention Mechanism for Knowledge Transfer Between Teacher and Student Networks
abstract: The process of knowledge distillation involves imparting the information acquired by a teacher network to a student network, enabling the student to maintain accuracy close to the teacher with fewer parameters and computational demands. This study introduces a novel distillation framework comprising two knowledge transmission techniques alongside a decay mechanism for the distillation loss. The first technique, termed channel-wise attention distillation, facilitates the transfer of channel-specific representations from teacher to student. The second, denoted as guided knowledge distillation, distinguishes itself from traditional knowledge distillation by restricting the student's imitation solely to the correct predictions of the teacher, rather than the full prediction distribution on each sample. Finally, an early decay strategy gradually reduces the influence of the distillation loss during training, allowing the student network to increasingly govern its own optimization process. Experimental validation on ImageNet and CIFAR100 datasets demonstrates the effectiveness of the approach: a top-1 error rate of 27.68% is attained on ImageNet using ResNet18, surpassing contemporary methods, while on CIFAR100, the student model achieves performance exceeding that of the teacher. The implementation is publicly accessible at https://github.com/zhouzaida/channel-distillation.

author: Gardner
title: Distillation Methods for Enhancing Adversarial Robustness in Neural Networks
abstract: This work explores the transfer of adversarial robustness in the context of knowledge distillation, a widely used technique for training compact neural classifiers. Although smaller networks obtained through distillation generally perform well on classification tasks, they remain susceptible to adversarial perturbations. Our investigation reveals that robustness can be significantly conveyed to the student model even when the distillation process utilizes exclusively unperturbed training samples. We propose a novel distillation framework designed to embed adversarial robustness into compact student architectures. This approach maintains the ability to generate small networks with strong predictive performance, comparable to traditional distillation, while also effectively transferring the enhanced robustness characteristics of larger teacher models. Experimental results demonstrate that students trained using this method consistently achieve higher robust accuracy than adversarially trained models sharing the same network architecture, outperforming current state-of-the-art techniques on established benchmarks evaluating robustness. Moreover, by incorporating recent advancements in efficient adversarial training strategies, we improve the training speed of our robust distillation approach, facilitating faster convergence of robust student models.

author: Robinson
title: Analyzing Ensemble Methods, Knowledge Distillation, and Self-Distillation in Deep Neural Networks
abstract: This work rigorously investigates how aggregating multiple deep learning models enhances test accuracy and explores the process of transferring this improved performance into a single model through knowledge distillation. We focus on the particularly difficult scenario in which the ensemble is formed by averaging outputs from several independently trained neural networks that share an identical architecture, training algorithm, and dataset, differing only in their random initialization seeds. Our findings reveal that ensemble techniques and knowledge distillation in deep neural networks behave fundamentally differently from classical learning frameworks like boosting or neural tangent kernels (NTKs). To better comprehend these phenomena, we propose a theoretical framework demonstrating that, under a data structure we define as "multi-view," combining independently trained neural networks can guarantee improved test accuracy. Furthermore, this enhanced accuracy can be certified to transfer to an individual model by training it to replicate the ensemble's output instead of fitting the true labels. These results provide a new perspective on ensemble utility in deep learning distinct from established theorems and clarify how the so-called "dark knowledge" embedded in ensemble outputs facilitates distillation. Finally, we establish that self-distillation effectively acts as an implicit fusion of ensemble averaging and knowledge distillation, leading to improved test accuracy.

author: Lawrence
title: Transferring Knowledge from a Deep Network for Pose Regression
abstract: We introduce an innovative approach for extracting knowledge from a deep pose regressor network aimed at improving efficiency in Visual Odometry (VO). Traditional distillation techniques depend on "dark knowledge" for effective transfer, which is absent in pose regression scenarios; additionally, the teacher's outputs can be unreliable. To address this, our method selectively prioritizes knowledge transfer based on the reliability of the teacher. This is implemented by employing the teacher's loss as a confidence measure that adjusts the influence of its predictions. This confidence is incorporated into the core training process through Attentive Imitation Loss (AIL) and during the acquisition of the teacher's intermediate features via Attentive Hint Training (AHT). To our knowledge, this represents the first successful endeavor to distill from a deep pose regression model. Experiments conducted on the KITTI and Malaga datasets demonstrate that the student model can maintain prediction accuracy close to that of the teacher while achieving up to 92.95% reduction in parameters and a computational speed increase by a factor of 2.12.

author: Pacheco
title: Adversarial Sample-Based Knowledge Transfer Emphasizing Classifier Decision Boundaries
abstract: Improving knowledge distillation remains a challenge despite numerous recent approaches enabling a trained neural network to guide the training of another model. Here, we introduce an alternative viewpoint that focuses on the decision boundary, a critical element defining the classifier's behavior. Since a classifier’s generalization ability is strongly influenced by how well its decision boundary is formed, effective knowledge transfer should involve information tied to this boundary. To accomplish this, we apply adversarial attacks that reveal boundary-supporting samples, which serve as a basis for transferring boundary-specific knowledge. The method we propose trains the student model utilizing these adversarial samples to enhance the fidelity of decision boundary information transmission. Our experimental evaluations confirm that this approach enhances the distillation process and attains performance surpassing current leading techniques.

author: Smith
title: Understanding Knowledge Distillation through Measurement of Encoded Knowledge
abstract: A technique is introduced to explain why knowledge distillation succeeds by measuring and examining the task-relevant and task-irrelevant visual concepts represented in the intermediate layers of a deep neural network (DNN). The study proposes three specific hypotheses: (1) training a DNN via knowledge distillation results in the acquisition of a larger number of visual concepts compared to training on raw data alone; (2) knowledge distillation encourages the DNN to acquire multiple visual concepts concurrently, in contrast to the sequential acquisition observed when learning directly from raw data; and (3) knowledge distillation produces more consistent optimization trajectories than training using only raw data. To test these claims, three categories of mathematical metrics are established to assess the DNN's feature representations. Experimental evaluation across various DNN architectures confirmed the validity of these hypotheses.

author: Shaffer
title: Targeted Sample Selection in Knowledge Distillation for Neural Machine Translation
abstract: State-of-the-art results have been achieved by Neural Machine Translation (NMT) systems across numerous benchmarks. Knowledge distillation remains a prominent technique in this domain, where the teacher model’s information is propagated via each training example to enhance the student model. Despite its prevalence, existing studies seldom address the varied effects and interrelations of these training examples, which act as conduits for transferring knowledge. This work introduces a new analytic framework designed to investigate the differential influence of training samples by contrasting multiple sample partitions. Utilizing this framework, comprehensive experiments reveal that increased knowledge transfer per sample does not necessarily translate to improved overall distillation outcomes; in fact, excessive focus on certain examples may degrade performance. Motivated by these insights, we develop two straightforward yet powerful selection mechanisms—operating at batch and global levels—to identify optimal samples for the distillation process. The methods are validated on two major machine translation benchmarks, WMT’14 English to German and WMT’19 Chinese to English, with results demonstrating improvements of up to +1.28 and +0.89 BLEU points over the Transformer baseline, respectively.

author: Wolfe
title: Efficient and Reliable Data-Free Knowledge Distillation via Generative Replay of Synthesized Samples
abstract: Knowledge Distillation (KD) without access to original training data enables transferring knowledge from a pretrained teacher network to a smaller student network. Typically, prior methods rely on a validation dataset to track student accuracy on real samples and report the highest accuracy observed. However, such validation data might not be accessible during distillation, preventing identification of the best-performing student checkpoint. Consequently, a practical data-free KD approach must not only be robust but also ideally yield steadily improving student accuracy throughout training. Achieving this is difficult due to distributional shifts in synthetic data causing student performance to degrade. A naive solution is to periodically save and rehearse generated synthetic samples, which increases memory requirements and raises privacy issues. To address this, we introduce a generative model that captures the distribution of previously synthesized samples. Specifically, we employ a Variational Autoencoder (VAE) trained with a tailored objective to optimally represent the synthetic data. The student network is refined through generative pseudo replay, where the VAE generates samples to rehearse, eliminating the need to store any actual data. Results on image classification benchmarks demonstrate that the proposed method maximizes the expected distilled model accuracy while avoiding the extensive memory usage associated with sample storage-based techniques.

author: Peterson
title: Analyzing the Role of Knowledge Distillation in Parallel Token Generation for Machine Translation
abstract: Non-autoregressive translation models generate all output tokens simultaneously, resulting in notable speedups relative to sequential autoregressive approaches. Typically, these models depend on knowledge distillation, wherein a pretrained autoregressive teacher model provides the training targets that enhance performance. Although knowledge distillation consistently yields significant accuracy improvements for non-autoregressive translation, the underlying cause of this effect has remained elusive. In this study, we conduct controlled experiments to elucidate the importance of knowledge distillation for training parallel translation models. Our results demonstrate that distillation simplifies dataset complexity and enables the model to better capture output variations. Additionally, we identify a strong relationship between the non-autoregressive model’s capacity and the distilled data’s optimal complexity needed to maximize translation accuracy. Leveraging these insights, we propose several methods to modify dataset complexity, thereby boosting non-autoregressive model effectiveness. Our methods establish new state-of-the-art results among non-autoregressive models and narrow the performance difference with autoregressive baselines on the WMT14 English-German benchmark.

author: Moore
title: Attention-Guided Feature Matching for Knowledge Distillation
abstract: Extracting broadly applicable information from a pre-trained teacher model to guide a student model forms the core of knowledge distillation. Traditional approaches often manually define intermediate feature correspondences between teacher and student networks, which can create suboptimal connections that hinder distillation gains. Although some efforts have been made to overcome these limitations, reliably identifying effective links remains difficult in real-world applications. This work proposes an efficient and effective feature distillation technique that leverages every hierarchical feature level from the teacher without requiring manual link specification. Central to our approach is an attention-driven meta-network that learns the relative affinities among features and employs these affinities to modulate distillation strengths over all possible feature pairs. Consequently, the proposed method selects useful connections more effectively than prior strategies and achieves superior results in model compression and transfer learning scenarios. Comprehensive qualitative assessments and ablation experiments elucidate the mechanisms by which our method enhances distillation quality. The source code can be accessed at github.com/clovaai/attention-feature-distillation.

author: Bernard
title: Dynamic Teacher Weighting via Reinforcement for Multi-Teacher Knowledge Distillation
abstract: Pre-trained deep models in natural language processing (NLP) frequently face challenges in deployment due to slow inference times and large GPU memory demands. Knowledge distillation, widely adopted for compressing models, involves transferring information from one or more large teacher models to a more compact student model. Current leading approaches in multi-teacher distillation typically assign fixed importance weights to each teacher throughout the distillation process. Moreover, many of these approaches treat all teacher models as equally influential. Our study highlights that, given the complexity of training data and variability in student model capacity, adaptively weighting the influence of teacher models on a per-example basis can improve student performance. To this end, we propose a reinforcement learning framework that dynamically adjusts teacher weights according to individual training instances, aiming to enhance student learning outcomes. Comprehensive experiments conducted across multiple NLP tasks demonstrate the practical benefits and robustness of our proposed technique.

author: Rogers
title: Multi-Teacher Knowledge Distillation Integrating Confidence Measures
abstract: Originally, knowledge distillation leverages supervision from a single teacher model to train a student model. To enhance student accuracy, recent approaches incorporate knowledge from multiple teachers. Nonetheless, current methods typically merge diverse teacher outputs by averaging predictions or other label-independent techniques, which can mislead the student when some teacher predictions are unreliable. To address this issue, the proposed method assigns sample-dependent confidence scores to each teacher prediction based on the ground-truth, emphasizing those predictions that approximate one-hot labels with higher weights. Moreover, it integrates features from intermediate layers to ensure a more stable knowledge transfer. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that this approach consistently surpasses all state-of-the-art baselines on various architectures for teacher-student frameworks.

author: Davis
title: Adversarial Training of Feature Map Distributions for Online Knowledge Distillation
abstract: While class probabilities have been the primary focus in earlier online knowledge distillation approaches, feature maps offer extensive data on image intensity and spatial relations that remain underexploited. This study introduces an online knowledge distillation technique that conveys knowledge from both class probabilities and feature maps through an adversarial training setup. Our approach involves simultaneous training of multiple networks, each paired with a discriminator that identifies feature map distributions, labeling its own network's feature maps as counterfeit and those from other networks as genuine. By encouraging a network to deceive its paired discriminator, it adopts the feature map distribution characteristics of other networks. Empirical evaluation demonstrates that this adversarial strategy surpasses traditional direct alignment methods like L1, showing greater effectiveness for online distillation. Furthermore, a novel cyclic training procedure is developed to enable collaborative learning involving more than two networks. Application across diverse network architectures on classification tasks highlights especially notable performance gains when training a small and a large network in tandem.

author: Abbott
title: Adversarial Framework for Knowledge Distillation in Deep Graph Neural Networks Compression
abstract: Graph neural networks (GNNs) of considerable depth have proven effective in representing graph-structured inputs. Yet, their deeply layered design complicates deployment and quick evaluation on mobile and embedded platforms. One promising approach to reduce complexity in deep GNNs involves knowledge distillation using teacher-student frameworks, where a critical aspect is quantifying the divergence between teacher and student models through fixed distance metrics. These fixed metrics, however, may inadequately capture discrepancies across diverse graph structures, and identifying the best metric remains challenging. To address these challenges, this work presents an adversarially trained knowledge distillation method tailored for graph models. This method jointly trains a discriminator and student GNN—interpreted as a generator—to dynamically assess and minimize differences between teacher and student outputs. Central to this approach is a discriminator that evaluates knowledge transfer from node-level and class-level perspectives, emphasizing the inter-node and inter-class relationships pivotal to deep GNN performance. The discriminator learns to differentiate teacher-generated knowledge from that acquired by the student, while the student attempts to deceive the discriminator. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first application of adversarial training within graph-based knowledge distillation. Empirical results on standard node and graph classification tasks confirm that the proposed adversarial method significantly enhances student GNN performance, demonstrating precise knowledge transfer from complex teacher models to smaller student architectures.

author: Munoz
title: Knowledge Distillation Without Access to Original Training Data in Deep Neural Networks
abstract: The task of knowledge distillation aims to train a compact Student model guided by a more complex Teacher model to preserve much of its effectiveness. Traditional solutions rely on the dataset or derived meta-data to educate the Student. Yet, it may be impractical to obtain the training set used by the Teacher due to its size or potential privacy and security issues, such as in biometric or medical contexts. To address this, we introduce a novel approach that does not require any data or meta-data, where representations called Data Impressions are generated directly from the intricate Teacher model to act as substitutes for the original training examples. These synthesized representations then facilitate knowledge transfer to the Student through distillation. We refer to this approach as Zero-Shot Knowledge Distillation and show that it achieves comparable generalization results to conventional distillation methods that depend on the actual training data across several widely used benchmarks.

author: Roman
title: Feature Distillation to Enhance Fairness in Visual Recognition Tasks
abstract: Addressing fairness concerns in computer vision, particularly within systems involving human-related decisions, remains a challenging pursuit. Ensuring that an algorithm yields unbiased results across protected groups has yet to be fully achieved. This study introduces a methodical technique aimed at diminishing algorithmic bias through feature distillation tailored for visual recognition problems, referred to here as the proposed method. While distillation methods are commonly employed to enhance predictive performance, we identify a lack of explicit efforts focusing on fairness improvement via distillation. Additionally, a theoretical analysis is provided to explain the influences of knowledge distillation on fairness outcomes. Comprehensive experimentation demonstrates that the proposed method effectively reduces bias affecting certain minority groups without compromising accuracy, validated on both artificially generated and authentic face image datasets.

author: Blair
title: An Analysis of Policy Knowledge Transfer Techniques
abstract: Knowledge transfer from a source policy to a target policy plays a crucial role in Deep Reinforcement Learning. Known as distillation, this approach has proven effective by improving agent optimisation and achieving accelerated and enhanced performance on more challenging tasks [26, 32, 5, 8]. Although distillation is commonly applied and straightforward in concept, a variety of different implementations exist, with subtle distinctions that can significantly impact both the attained objectives and empirical outcomes. We conduct a thorough investigation of the policy distillation domain, evaluating the theoretical foundations and empirical benefits of multiple variants. Our findings identify three preferred distillation methods contingent on task characteristics. Notably, one method based on expected entropy regularisation facilitates faster acquisition of policies across diverse scenarios while maintaining convergence guarantees.

author: Herrera
title: Enhancing Object Detector Compression via Detailed Feature Response Mimicry
abstract: Deploying advanced CNN recognition systems on resource-constrained devices remains challenging due to computational demands. Knowledge distillation offers a compelling solution by training a smaller student model to replicate the outputs of a more complex teacher, thereby boosting generalization. Despite success in classification, this approach has limited effectiveness for object detection tasks. We demonstrate that naive knowledge distillation applied directly to detection yields only marginal improvements. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a technique based on precise feature response imitation, focusing on the spatial variation of activation differences. Our key insight is that detectors primarily prioritize local regions adjacent to objects; hence, discrepancies in feature responses near object-related anchor positions provide valuable cues about the teacher’s generalization behavior. We develop a novel strategy for identifying these critical locations and enforce student model mimicry specifically at these points, resulting in improved detection performance. The approach is initially validated on a streamlined toy detector embodying fundamental principles of leading anchor-based detection architectures, using the challenging KITTI dataset. Here, our method achieves an increase in mAP up to 15% relative to a non-imitated baseline student. Further comprehensive experiments involving Faster R-CNN across diverse settings with Pascal VOC and COCO benchmarks indicate that this feature imitation significantly mitigates performance degradation, recovering up to 74% of the student model’s accuracy loss compared to the teacher. Code implementations are publicly available at https://github.com/twangnh/Distilling-Object-Detectors

author: Dudley
title: Distillation of Ensemble Knowledge Using Attention for Machine Reading Comprehension
abstract: Although substantial progress has been made by current reading comprehension models, these improvements usually rely on ensembles of multiple models. Additionally, such methods remain susceptible to adversarial manipulations. This study addresses these issues by utilizing knowledge distillation to convey knowledge from ensemble models to a single network. Initially, we show that standard knowledge distillation focused on answer span prediction benefits reading comprehension architectures. Building on this, we introduce two innovative techniques that simultaneously discourage incorrect predictions on confounding answers and incorporate alignment-based guidance derived from the ensemble during training. Our experiments reveal that the optimized student model experiences only a minimal decrease of 0.4% in F1 on the SQuAD test dataset relative to the ensemble teacher, while achieving a 12-fold speedup in inference. Furthermore, it surpasses the teacher's performance on adversarial SQuAD variants and the NarrativeQA dataset.

author: Gray
title: Progressive Substitution of Modules for BERT Compression
abstract: We introduce an innovative technique for compressing BERT that relies on gradually substituting the original modules with their smaller counterparts. Initially, the original BERT model is partitioned into multiple segments, each paired with a compressed version. These compressed modules are trained by intermittently swapping them in place of the original modules so they learn to replicate their functionality. The frequency of these substitutions is steadily raised as training proceeds, fostering increasing interaction between the full-sized and compact models. Unlike prior knowledge distillation methods used for reducing BERT, this technique avoids the use of any additional loss terms. Evaluated on the GLUE benchmark, our method surpasses existing distillation-based compression strategies, offering an alternative framework for model size reduction.

author: Arnold
title: Evaluating the Effectiveness of Knowledge Distillation
abstract: Training a compact student network to replicate the behavior of a larger teacher model, including ensembles, is a common application of knowledge distillation. Our findings reveal that although knowledge distillation can enhance the student's generalization abilities, it frequently does not function in the way traditionally assumed: there often exists a significant gap between the predictive outputs of teacher and student models, even when the student is theoretically capable of exactly reproducing the teacher. We attribute this mismatch chiefly to optimization challenges that prevent the student from fully aligning with the teacher. Furthermore, we demonstrate that characteristics of the distillation dataset influence the degree of similarity attained between teacher and student; intriguingly, achieving closer alignment does not invariably result in superior generalization by the student.

author: Calderon
title: Knowledge Distillation for Developing Generalizable Deep Models in Vehicle Routing Problems
abstract: Neural approaches applied to vehicle routing problems typically undergo training and evaluation on identical instance distributions, usually uniform. Addressing the issue of cross-distribution generalization, we introduce knowledge distillation into this domain and design an Adaptive Multi-Distribution Knowledge Distillation framework to facilitate the training of deep models that generalize better. This framework integrates knowledge from several teacher models, each trained on distinct exemplar distributions, enabling the creation of a compact yet versatile student model. Moreover, it includes an adaptive mechanism guiding the student to focus learning on challenging distributions to efficiently assimilate complex knowledge. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that our approach attains performance comparable to existing neural baselines on both seen and unseen distributions, including those generated randomly and sourced from standard benchmarks such as TSPLIB and CVRPLIB. Importantly, this method is broadly applicable and demands fewer computational resources during inference.

author: Montgomery
title: 3D Object Detection from Point Clouds via Dynamic Graph-Based Message Passing
abstract: Addressing 3D object detection typically demands complex training and evaluation sequences that rely heavily on expertise specific to datasets. Drawing motivation from recent 2D detectors that eliminate non-maximum suppression, we introduce a 3D detection framework designed for point cloud inputs. This framework interprets 3D object detection as message propagation within a dynamically constructed graph, extending the DGCNN model to output multiple object predictions. Our design obviates the need for steps such as non-maximum suppression or confidence-based post-processing of detected objects. To enable robust detection when working with sparse point clouds, we develop a specialized set-to-set distillation technique tailored for this 3D detection scenario. This technique enforces permutation-invariant alignment between the outputs of a teacher and a student model, greatly streamlining the knowledge distillation process for 3D detection tasks. Evaluated on autonomous driving datasets, our approach attains leading results, alongside providing comprehensive analyses of both the detection system and the distillation method.

author: Hensley
title: Enhancing Accuracy of Low-Precision Networks via Knowledge Distillation Approaches
abstract: State-of-the-art results in computer vision tasks such as image classification and object detection have been attained by deep learning models. However, these high-performing architectures frequently consist of very large networks with many parameters. Deploying these top-tier models on inference devices with limited computational and memory resources remains difficult, as these deep or wide networks demand substantial computation and storage. Techniques like model compression through knowledge distillation and the use of low-precision arithmetic are widely adopted to reduce both computational load and memory use for deployment. This work explores the synergy of combining low-precision numerics with knowledge distillation, demonstrating that distillation significantly enhances the accuracy of networks operating at reduced precision levels. The proposed method achieves leading accuracy with ternary and 4-bit precision for different ResNet variants evaluated on the ImageNet benchmark. Furthermore, we introduce three different strategies for integrating knowledge distillation at multiple steps within the training and deployment workflow.

author: Ray
title: Transferring the Influence of Inductive Bias via Knowledge Distillation
abstract: Inductive biases play a vital role in tasks or situations characterized by constraints in available data or computational power, as well as when the training distribution does not match test conditions. Nonetheless, the formulation, design, and effective adaptation of inductive biases often present challenges. This work investigates the utilization of knowledge distillation to convey the influence of inductive biases from a source model to a target model. We analyze model families exhibiting distinct inductive biases—specifically LSTMs versus Transformers and CNNs versus MLPs—in contexts where selecting appropriate inductive biases is essential. Our study examines the impact of inductive biases on the solutions toward which models converge and assesses the degree and manner in which knowledge distillation transfers these inductive bias effects, evaluating both performance outcomes and qualitative properties of the final solutions.

author: Bush
title: Enhancing Multi-Label Image Classification through Knowledge Transfer from Weakly-Supervised Object Detection
abstract: The task of multi-label image classification remains a crucial yet difficult problem for comprehensive visual recognition. Prior approaches have demonstrated that region-based information, such as features extracted from RoIs, can enhance classification accuracy. However, these techniques often depend on detailed object-level annotations, including exact object categories and bounding box coordinates, which are costly to obtain. In this work, we introduce an effective and streamlined deep learning framework that leverages knowledge distillation from a weakly-supervised detection model that operates without bounding box labels to improve multi-label classification. Concretely, starting from image-level labels, we (1) train a weakly-supervised detection network, followed by (2) designing an end-to-end multi-label classification architecture incorporating a knowledge distillation component. This component transfers guidance from the weakly-supervised detector—serving as the teacher—to the classifier—acting as the student—based on the image-level class predictions and object-level RoI features. Once the distillation process is complete, the classification model benefits from notable performance gains while preserving inference efficiency since the teacher network is discarded during testing. Comprehensive evaluations on two prominent large-scale benchmarks, MS-COCO and NUS-WIDE, demonstrate that the proposed method surpasses current top-performing approaches in both accuracy and computational efficiency.

author: Williams
title: Relational Knowledge Distillation for Link Prediction Without Link Features
abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have achieved remarkable results in link prediction tasks, yet their practical use is hindered by the substantial inference latency caused by complex neighborhood dependencies. In contrast, MLPs provide faster inference but fall short in effectiveness due to the absence of relational information. To merge the benefits of both models, this study investigates direct knowledge distillation approaches, including alignment of predicted logits and node embeddings, for link prediction. Finding these direct distillation techniques insufficient, we introduce a new relational distillation paradigm designed to transfer relational knowledge concentrated around each anchor node to the student MLP. Our approach employs two complementary methods: rank-based matching and distribution-based matching. Comprehensive evaluations reveal that this method significantly improves MLP link prediction accuracy, surpassing teacher GNNs on seven out of eight datasets, and achieves a 70.68-fold acceleration in inference speed over GNNs on the large-scale OGB benchmark.

author: Perez
title: Unsupervised Domain Adaptation Utilizing One or Multiple Black-box Source Models
abstract: Unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) seeks to leverage knowledge from prior labeled datasets (sources) to an unlabeled target dataset to reduce annotation costs. Most existing approaches require access to original source data and implement alignment strategies that depend on those data to identify target domain instances under a transductive paradigm, which can introduce privacy risks concerning the source subjects. Some recently proposed methods address this concern by employing source domain white-box models, but these can still potentially expose raw data through adversarial generative frameworks. This work investigates a realistic and novel UDA scenario where adaptation occurs with only black-box source predictors accessible, meaning just the output predictions of the source network are available for the target domain. To tackle this challenge, we introduce a novel two-phase knowledge transfer mechanism named the proposed method. Initially, it distills information from the source black-box predictor into a tailored target domain model, then subsequently fine-tunes this distilled model to better accommodate the target distribution. Additionally, the method permits neural networks with differing architectures between source and target, supporting efficient adaptation including on resource-limited devices. Experimental validation across three UDA cases—single-source, multi-source, and partial-set adaptation—demonstrates that the proposed method attains performance on par with leading data-dependent techniques.

author: Roberts
title: Enhancing Deep Neural Network Explainability via Knowledge Distillation
abstract: Deep Neural Networks have propelled advancements across diverse fields including speech recognition, computer vision, and language modeling. Despite their high accuracy, mere performance is insufficient for deployment scenarios that require interpretability, especially in ethical or critical mission contexts. The inherent complexity of Deep Neural Network architectures obstructs transparent interpretation and comprehensibility of their outputs, limiting their broader applicability. To address this challenge, we use Knowledge Distillation to transfer knowledge from Deep Neural Networks into decision trees, aiming for a balance between interpretability and predictive accuracy. We treat this task as a multi-output regression challenge, and empirical results indicate that the distilled student models surpass standard decision trees in accuracy by approximately 1% to 5% given equal tree depth. Our experiments, conducted using TensorFlow, ensure scalability for large-scale datasets. Notably, this work is the first to perform distillation of Deep Neural Networks into standard decision trees specifically on multi-class classification datasets.

author: Miller
title: Analyzing the Effect of Distillation on BERT-Based Ranking Models
abstract: Pretrained deep language models like BERT have significantly advanced the performance of top-tier information retrieval ranking architectures. These models are capable of capturing intricate relevance signals between queries and passages thanks to their embedded knowledge. Nonetheless, the computational expense at inference time often restricts their practical use in real-world search applications. This work investigates the transfer process of search-related knowledge from BERT to a more compact ranking model via distillation. Results indicate that employing an appropriate distillation strategy is essential, achieving up to a ninefold increase in speed without sacrificing state-of-the-art ranking quality.

author: Hall
title: Zero-Shot Knowledge Transfer for Federated Learning with Diverse On-Device Models under Limited Device Resources
abstract: In federated learning, multiple distributed devices collaborate to train a unified prediction model without pooling their local data centrally. Prevailing methods typically mandate uniform local training efforts across devices with identical model architectures and sizes, creating barriers for devices with limited computational capabilities. Addressing the prevalence of diverse device types, we introduce a novel federated learning framework supporting heterogeneous on-device architectures through a zero-shot knowledge transfer mechanism, referred to here as the proposed method. This approach empowers each device to select its model configuration based on available local computational resources. To facilitate knowledge transmission among these varied models, we develop a zero-shot distillation technique that operates without relying on private local data, contrasting with earlier approaches dependent on public datasets or pretrained data generators. Additionally, the computationally demanding distillation operation is centralized on the server, enabling devices with limited resources to participate effectively; the server trains a generator adversarially using an ensemble of the aggregated on-device models. The resulting distilled global knowledge is subsequently dispatched as tailored on-device model parameters, which devices can integrate with ease. Comprehensive experiments validate that the proposed method is effective and robust when addressing model heterogeneity, device-agnostic knowledge transfer, and complex federated learning conditions, including variable local data distributions and straggler phenomena.

author: Garcia
title: Reducing the Size of Visual-linguistic Models through Knowledge Distillation
abstract: While substantial advancements exist in pre-training visual-linguistic (VL) models, few works focus on producing compact VL architectures. This study investigates knowledge distillation (KD) as a strategy to downscale a large transformer-based VL model to a smaller one. A key difficulty stems from the mismatch of regional visual tokens generated by distinct object detectors in the Teacher and Student models, causing divergence in hidden layer features and attention maps. To overcome this, we retrain the Teacher model utilizing the Student's detector region proposals, combined with features derived from the Teacher’s own detector, ensuring input alignment. This adaptation enables effective knowledge transfer via intermediate activations. Concretely, we apply a mean squared error loss to replicate the transformer’s internal attention patterns and introduce a token-level noise contrastive loss to align hidden states by discriminating against negative embeddings maintained in a sample queue. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed distillation technique yields substantial gains for smaller VL models on both image captioning and visual question answering benchmarks. Specifically, the compact model achieves a CIDEr score of 120.8 on COCO captioning, exceeding the undistilled model by 5.1 points, and an accuracy of 69.8 on the VQA 2.0 dataset, improving 0.8 over the baseline. Comprehensive experiments and ablation studies validate the positive impact of VL distillation during both pre-training and downstream fine-tuning.

author: Ramirez
title: Progressive Refinement of Self-Distilled Targets for Model Training
abstract: Enhancements in deep neural network generalization have been achieved through numerous regularization approaches, such as limiting function complexity, incorporating noise during training, and data augmentation. This study introduces a straightforward but potent regularization technique referred to as progressive self-knowledge distillation, which incrementally refines a model’s self-generated knowledge to relax the standard one-hot target labels throughout training. This approach aligns with knowledge distillation frameworks where the student simultaneously assumes the role of the teacher. Concretely, the method adaptively modifies the training targets by integrating the true labels with the model’s earlier output predictions. We demonstrate that this progressive self-distillation method effectively performs hard example mining by modulating gradient magnitudes based on classification difficulty. The approach is universally applicable to supervised tasks utilizing hard target labels and can be seamlessly combined with pre-existing regularization strategies to boost generalization. Additionally, it is empirically validated that this method yields superior accuracy alongside improved confidence calibration and ordinal ranking quality. Comprehensive experiments across image classification, object detection, and machine translation domains illustrate consistent enhancement over leading baseline models. The implementation code is accessible at https://github.com/lgcnsai/PS-KD-Pytorch.

author: Reid
title: Efficient Distillation through Low-Cost Convolutional Adaptations
abstract: Deploying contemporary neural network models in environments with restricted memory remains challenging, as versatile techniques for memory reduction are not well developed and their trade-offs are poorly understood. We introduce a structural distillation approach aimed at decreasing memory requirements by creating a student model which is a straightforward modification of the teacher network: this approach avoids architectural redesign and allows retention of identical hyperparameters. By employing attention transfer, we generate Pareto fronts and tabular data characterizing the trade-off between memory use and accuracy for residual network distillation across four established benchmark datasets. Our findings demonstrate that significant reductions in memory consumption can be achieved with minimal accuracy degradation. Moreover, we verify that student models trained via distillation outperform those trained solely on the original data without teacher guidance.

author: Diaz
title: Two-phase Multi-teacher Knowledge Distillation Approach for Compressing Models in Web-based Question Answering Systems
abstract: Extensive pre-training followed by fine-tuning of models such as BERT and OpenAI GPT has achieved impressive outcomes in question answering tasks. Nevertheless, their large number of parameters result in slow inference speeds, posing difficulties in deploying these sophisticated models in practical business environments. Conventional approaches to model compression often incur significant information degradation during the compression process, causing the compressed models to perform worse than the original ones. To address this issue, the proposed method introduces a Two-stage Multi-teacher Knowledge Distillation technique tailored for web Question Answering systems. Initially, a general Question & Answer distillation task is used to pre-train the student model. Subsequently, this student model undergoes fine-tuning via multi-teacher knowledge distillation on downstream datasets including Web Q&A, MNLI, SNLI, and RTE from GLUE. This strategy reduces overfitting tendencies found in individual teacher models and conveys broader knowledge to the student model. Experimental findings demonstrate that our approach surpasses baseline techniques considerably and reaches performance levels comparable to the initial teacher models, while greatly enhancing inference speed.

author: Wood
title: A Statistical Analysis of Effective Data Augmentation Strategies in Knowledge Distillation
abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) leverages a teacher network to assist the training of a student network. While prior work predominantly focuses on the output side of KD, such as optimizing loss functions, limited efforts have examined the role of input transformations, particularly data augmentation (DA), in KD. This study investigates why certain DA techniques, like CutMix, yield superior results within KD frameworks, aiming to define what constitutes an effective DA for KD. From a statistical viewpoint, our findings indicate that successful DA methods reduce the covariance observed in the teacher-student cross-entropy loss. We propose a quantifiable indicator—the standard deviation of the teacher’s average predicted probability (T. stddev)—and validate its effectiveness through empirical evidence. Alongside this theoretical insight, we present an entropy-driven data mixing augmentation approach named CutMixPick, designed to improve upon existing CutMix performance. Comprehensive experiments validate our theoretical propositions and show that strategically selecting DA methods can substantially boost KD outcomes.

author: Clark
title: Encoder-Decoder Filter Reduction via Collaborative Knowledge Transfer for Ultra-Resolution Style Adaptation
abstract: Methods enabling universal style transfer frequently exploit representations derived from deep CNN architectures (such as VGG-19) pretrained on extensive image datasets. However, deploying these approaches for ultra-high-resolution imagery is severely limited due to the significant model size and associated memory demands. We introduce a knowledge distillation technique tailored for encoder-decoder neural style transfer frameworks to compress convolutional filters. This approach is motivated by the observation that encoder-decoder pairs exhibit a distinctive cooperative interaction, which we interpret as novel transferable knowledge specific to style transfer networks. To address discrepancies in feature dimensions encountered during the distillation process, we propose a linear embedding loss that encourages the student network to approximate a linear projection of the teacher’s feature space. Comprehensive evaluations demonstrate our approach’s effectiveness across various universal style transfer methods—including WCT and AdaIN—while achieving up to a 15.5-fold reduction in model size. Notably, utilizing compressed models with WCT, we realize ultra-resolution universal style transfer exceeding 40 megapixels on a 12GB GPU, a first in the field. Additional testing on optimization-based stylization frameworks highlights the broad applicability of the proposed method across distinct style transfer paradigms. Our implementation and pretrained models are publicly accessible at https://github.com/mingsun-tse/collaborative-distillation.

author: Adams
title: Examining Deep Learning Practices: The Roles of Learning Rate Restarts, Warmup Procedures, and Knowledge Distillation
abstract: Deep learning model training benefits considerably from heuristics including learning rate scheduling, knowledge distillation, skip connections, and normalization layers, which enhance both convergence speed and ultimate performance. Due to the lack of comprehensive theoretical explanations, conducting carefully designed experiments can provide insights into the training dynamics and loss landscapes of these models. Prior empirical studies have mostly utilized linear interpolation and dimensionality reduction visualizations, each limited in scope. We instead apply recent techniques focused on loss surface and representation structure—specifically mode connectivity and canonical correlation analysis (CCA)—to reassess these heuristics. Concentrating on knowledge distillation alongside learning rate strategies such as cosine restart and warmup, our experiments reveal: (a) evidence does not support the commonly suggested explanations for the effectiveness of cosine annealing; (b) learning rate warmup primarily acts to stabilize training by avoiding disruption in the deeper layers; and (c) knowledge transferred from the teacher is predominantly absorbed in the deeper layers' latent representations.

author: Zuniga
title: Scaling neural network training across distributed systems via concurrent distillation
abstract: Ensembling and distillation methods provide improvements in model accuracy applicable to nearly any foundational architecture, yet industrial adoption is hindered by elevated inference costs for ensembles and the intricate training procedures required for distillation. We investigate a streamlined variation of distillation that avoids complex multi-phase training and the introduction of numerous hyperparameters, facilitating practical application. Our primary observation is that employing this online distillation approach allows exploitation of additional parallel computational resources, resulting in roughly a twofold acceleration in processing extremely large datasets. Notably, training speed gains persist beyond the limits where further parallelization no longer benefits standard synchronous or asynchronous stochastic gradient descent methods. This method involves two neural models trained separately on distinct data partitions, which exchange knowledge by pushing each to align with the other’s predicted outputs. These outputs may be generated from a lagging snapshot of the peer model, permitting infrequent weight communication without loss of effectiveness. Additionally, we demonstrate that the proposed online distillation technique substantially improves the cost-efficiency of producing highly consistent model predictions. Empirical validation is performed through experiments on the Criteo Display Ad Challenge, ImageNet, and the largest neural language modeling corpus to date, featuring 6 × 10^{11} tokens derived from the Common Crawl web dataset.

author: Wong
title: Utilizing Regularized Knowledge Distillation to Enhance Domain Generalization
abstract: Convolutional neural networks, despite their extensive use across various applications, often suffer from limited generalization when training data is insufficient or lacks diversity, posing challenges for real-world deployment. We introduce a straightforward and adaptable training approach based on knowledge distillation designed for domain generalization, incorporating a novel regularization component termed the gradient filter. Our study demonstrates that leveraging the teacher model's comprehensive dark knowledge alongside the newly introduced gradient filter facilitates easier learning of input-output mappings, thereby boosting the model's ability to generalize. Through comprehensive experiments across diverse tasks such as image classification, segmentation, and reinforcement learning, we show that the proposed approach markedly outperforms leading domain generalization methods. Furthermore, we recommend evaluating our method using two specific metrics to elucidate the mechanisms through which it enhances neural networks' generalization performance.

author: Lynch
title: Reevaluating Knowledge Distillation through the Lens of Label Smoothing Regularization
abstract: The objective of Knowledge Distillation (KD) is to transfer knowledge from a complex teacher model into a simpler student model. Conventionally, its effectiveness is attributed to the teacher providing privileged insights about inter-class similarities, which is why typically only competent teacher models instruct less capable students. Contrary to this prevailing notion, our experimental findings reveal two points: first, rather than solely the teacher aiding the student, the student can substantially refine the teacher by reversing the KD direction; second, even when the teacher is poorly trained and exhibits much lower accuracy than the student, it can still notably enhance the student’s performance. To elucidate these phenomena, we present a theoretical investigation connecting KD to label smoothing regularization. We demonstrate that KD can be viewed as a form of learned label smoothing regularization and that label smoothing itself acts as a surrogate teacher within KD. From these findings, we propose that the efficacy of KD does not solely stem from category similarity information conveyed by teachers but is also critically dependent on the regularization effect of soft targets, which plays an equally or more significant role. Building on this theoretical insight, we introduce a novel framework for Teacher-free Knowledge Distillation (Tf-KD), where the student model learns from either itself or a manually specified regularization distribution. The Tf-KD framework matches the performance of standard KD employing a superior teacher, enabling its practical application when stronger teacher models are not accessible. Furthermore, Tf-KD is versatile and can be straightforwardly utilized in training deep neural networks. Without incurring additional computational overhead, Tf-KD attains up to a 0.65% improvement on ImageNet relative to strong baseline models, outperforming conventional label smoothing regularization.

author: Jackson
title: Mutual Contrastive Learning for Collaborative Online Knowledge Distillation in Visual Recognition
abstract: Online Knowledge Distillation (KD) without teachers aims at a set of student models learning together, exchanging knowledge in real time. Prior online KD approaches typically emphasize class probability outputs, often disregarding the critical feature representation information. We introduce a framework based on Mutual Contrastive Learning (MCL) designed for online KD scenarios. The method hinges on the reciprocal exchange and compression of contrastive distributions between a group of networks simultaneously. By consolidating embedding information across networks, our framework maximizes a lower bound on mutual information between pairs of networks, allowing each model to acquire additional contrastive insights. This process enhances feature representations and yields superior outcomes in visual recognition tasks. Extending beyond only the final layer, the framework applies MCL to intermediate layers utilizing a meta-optimization-trained adaptive layer-alignment strategy. Evaluations on image classification and transfer learning tasks demonstrate that this layer-wise MCL consistently surpasses current state-of-the-art online KD methods in performance. These findings verify that layer-wise MCL effectively fosters improved feature representation learning. The implementation is accessible at https://github.com/winycg/L-MCL.

author: Daniel
title: Adversarial Model Compression Without Original Data
abstract: In recent years, Knowledge Distillation (KD) has advanced significantly, becoming a widely used framework for transferring knowledge and compressing models. Most KD techniques, however, depend on access to large original or substitute datasets, which are often inaccessible in practical situations. Addressing this limitation, we develop a new adversarial distillation framework enabling the creation of a small student network entirely without leveraging real data. We define a model discrepancy to quantitatively assess the gap between teacher and student networks and derive an optimizable upper limit on this metric. Within this framework, the teacher and student collaborate as a discriminator aiming to minimize the discrepancy, while a generator adversarially creates challenging inputs that maximize it. Comprehensive evaluations reveal that our data-free approach matches the accuracy of traditional data-dependent distillation strategies. Furthermore, our technique generalizes seamlessly to the more complex task of semantic segmentation, attaining state-of-the-art performance. Implementation details and pretrained models can be found at https://github.com/VainF/Data-Free-Adversarial-Distillation.

author: Martin
title: Transferring BERT Knowledge to Sequence-to-Sequence Models for ASR via Knowledge Distillation
abstract: Sequence-to-sequence models with attention have demonstrated strong performance in automatic speech recognition (ASR), but their left-to-right decoding restricts access to future context. To incorporate both preceding and succeeding context, we apply knowledge distillation from BERT—used as an external language model—to sequence-to-sequence ASR models. In this approach, soft targets produced by BERT supervise the training of the ASR model. Additionally, BERT is provided with context that extends beyond the current utterance. Experimental results on the Corpus of Spontaneous Japanese (CSJ) show significant ASR improvements over the seq2seq baseline. Distillation from BERT yields better outcomes than distillation from a transformer language model limited to left context. We further demonstrate the benefit of involving context outside the immediate utterance. Compared to other language model integration techniques such as n-best rescoring and shallow fusion, the proposed method delivers superior performance without adding inference time overhead.

author: Gray
title: Enhancing Feature Distillation Through Multiple Projector Networks
abstract: Feature distillation within knowledge distillation research has mainly concentrated on crafting loss functions and selecting which layers to distill, yet the role of the feature projector connecting teacher and student remains insufficiently examined. This study initiates by empirically investigating a plausible function of the projector and subsequently introduces a novel feature distillation approach that incorporates a set of projectors to boost student model performance. We find that incorporating a projector benefits the student network even when the feature dimensionality aligns between teacher and student. When the student backbone is trained without a projector, it can be viewed as conduction of multitask learning that simultaneously aims to extract discriminative features for classification and align features with the teacher for distillation. Our hypothesis, supported by empirical observations, is that absent a projector, student networks are prone to overfitting the teacher's feature distributions despite differences in architecture and initialization, which degrades the fidelity of student deep features used for classification. Including a projector effectively decouples these tasks, enabling the student to concentrate more on extracting primary features while still leveraging teacher-derived information via the projector. Building on these findings, we recommend employing an ensemble of projectors to further enhance student feature quality. Comprehensive experiments across various datasets and teacher-student configurations demonstrate the efficacy of this proposed approach.

author: Mayo
title: A Bias and Variance Analysis of Soft Label Utilization in Knowledge Distillation
abstract: The technique of knowledge distillation employs a pre-trained model or an ensemble, referred to as the teacher, to supervise the learning of a student network through soft label outputs. Soft labels from the teacher serve as training targets for the student network. Prior work has identified that softening labels acts as an effective form of regularization. While regularization traditionally reduces variance in statistical learning, the detailed effects on bias and variance when training with softened labels remain unclear. In this study, we examine how soft label distillation influences the bias-variance tradeoff, revealing that this tradeoff fluctuates on a per-sample basis during training. Additionally, when applying a fixed distillation temperature, we find an inverse correlation between distillation success and the count of certain samples, which we term regularization samples due to their role in increasing bias and decreasing variance. However, removing these regularization samples entirely causes a drop in distillation effectiveness, as demonstrated by our experiments. Motivated by these insights, we introduce a method of weighted soft labels that allows the model to adaptively balance the bias-variance tradeoff for each sample. Empirical results on benchmark datasets confirm the proposed method's benefits. The implementation is accessible at https://github.com/bellymonster/Weighted-Soft-Label-Distillation.

author: Bowman
title: Compressed Universal Paralinguistic Speech Embeddings via Knowledge Distillation
abstract: Advances in self-supervised learning have substantially enhanced the fidelity of speech embeddings. Nonetheless, implementing leading embedding architectures on consumer hardware remains challenging due to their scarce public release and extensive computational demands. To mitigate these challenges, we release a suite of compact paralinguistic speech models that closely match state-of-the-art effectiveness.
