Our methodology relies exclusively on knowledge distillation performed with publicly accessible datasets. We assess multiple model designs and conduct comprehensive evaluations on the Non-Semantic Speech (NOSS) benchmark. The largest compressed model occupies less than 15% of the original's storage (314MB compared to 2.2GB), attains over 96% accuracy on six out of seven benchmarked tasks, and trains on just 6.5% of the original training data. The smallest variant comprises only 1% of the original size (22MB) while achieving over 90% accuracy on the same six tasks. Across six of seven evaluation tasks, our models surpass the performance of the open source Wav2Vec 2.0 model. Notably, on both emotion recognition tasks, our most compact model outperforms Wav2Vec 2.0 despite having only 7% of its size.

author: Hawkins
title: An Accelerated Knowledge Distillation Scheme for Visual Recognition Tasks
abstract: Knowledge Distillation (KD) is widely applied in visual domains including supervised classification and self-supervised representation learning. Nevertheless, the standard KD approach suffers from high computational cost predominantly due to repeated forward passes through large teacher networks, which limits learning efficiency. A recent approach introduces a complete label map for the entire image, using RoI alignment on this precomputed label map to extract region-specific supervision during training without querying the teacher repeatedly. Despite this advantage, when the teachers are trained with multi-crop strategies, discrepancies arise between the global label map and region-level labels, leading to degraded performance. We propose a Fast Knowledge Distillation (FKD) framework that emulates the multi-crop KD training phase and generates soft labels while eliminating the need for runtime RoI align and softmax computations, resulting in faster training compared to this previous method. Implementing multi-crop data loading on the same image, FKD achieves greater computational efficiency than classic image classification pipelines. Experimental results on ImageNet-1K demonstrate our method attains 79.8% accuracy with ResNet-50, surpassing the earlier approach by approximately 1.0% margin with improved speed. Furthermore, FKD reveals notable efficiency benefits in self-supervised learning scenarios. The project website and resources including source code and pretrained models are accessible at the provided URLs.

author: Cohen
title: Attention-Guided Layer Combination Strategy for Enhancing Knowledge Distillation
abstract: In training and compressing neural networks, knowledge distillation involves jointly training two models, a teacher and a student, where the student attempts to replicate the teacher's outputs. Typically, to compress the model size while maintaining strong performance, the student features a simpler architecture. Distillation generally targets only the final output layer, despite the potential advantages of transferring supervisory signals from the teacher’s internal layers. Addressing this, we investigated intermediate layer distillation challenges, noting that the lack of direct one-to-one mapping between teacher and student layers leads prior methods to omit certain teacher layers and distill only a selected subset. This restriction negatively affects performance. We introduce a new method leveraging attention mechanisms to integrate multiple teacher layers, weighting each layer based on its relevance before transferring knowledge to the student’s layers. Applying this approach, we distilled a 12-layer BERT model into 6-, 4-, and 2-layer versions and tested them on several GLUE benchmark tasks. The results demonstrate that our attention-based fusion method surpasses previous distillation techniques in effectiveness.

author: Cameron
title: The Impact of Pre-training on Compact Model Performance in Language Tasks
abstract: Advancements in language representation have been dominated by large-scale, resource-intensive models trained on extensive general-domain corpora through self-supervised objectives. Given the computational burden of utilizing such models for downstream applications, various compression strategies have been developed for these pre-trained language models. Nevertheless, the straightforward approach of directly pre-training smaller models and then fine-tuning them has been largely neglected. Here, we demonstrate that pre-training is crucial even for architectures of limited capacity, and that fine-tuned compact pre-trained models achieve results comparable to more complex recent methods. Building on these pre-trained compact models, we investigate task knowledge transfer from large fine-tuned teacher models via conventional knowledge distillation. This straightforward yet powerful method, referred to as pre-trained distillation, yields additional performance improvements. Through comprehensive experimentation, we examine how pre-training and knowledge distillation interact with respect to two often overlooked factors: the scale of the model and characteristics of unlabeled task-specific data. Notably, a compounded influence emerges when these techniques are sequentially applied on the identical dataset. To facilitate continued investigation, we will release 24 small-scale pre-trained BERT models publicly.

author: Parsons
title: Applying Curriculum Learning to Enhance Distillation for Dense Retrieval Models
abstract: Distillation of ranking insights from a base re-ranking teacher model has recently been proven effective for improving dense retrieval models. This study introduces an adaptable curriculum learning optimization approach that modulates the hardness of teacher-generated training samples integrated into the distillation process. The proposed method gradually escalates the complexity of supervision signals by initially offering the student model broad preference pairs derived from the teacher's rankings and subsequently transitioning to demands on finer-grained pairwise ordering of documents. We demonstrate the utility of a straightforward variant of this curriculum learning framework when applied to refine two leading dense retrieval architectures. Validation on three widely-used passage retrieval benchmarks confirms the advantages of our approach.

author: Perez
title: Multi-Task Networks Improved via Iterative Single-Task Model Distillation for Natural Language Understanding
abstract: Training multi-task neural networks that exceed or even equal the performance of individual single-task models remains difficult. To tackle this issue, we introduce a technique where multiple single-task models act as instructors to a multi-task network through knowledge distillation. We further refine training with a novel procedure called teacher annealing, which progressively shifts the focus from distillation to direct supervised learning, enabling the multi-task network to outperform its single-task teachers. Using BERT fine-tuned on the GLUE benchmark in a multi-task setting, we demonstrate that our method outperforms both conventional single-task and multi-task training approaches.

author: Stewart
title: Differentially Private Compression of Neural Networks through Knowledge Distillation
abstract: Deploying high-capacity deep neural networks (DNNs) on mobile platforms is increasingly demanded to support advanced intelligent applications. Nevertheless, the superior capabilities of DNNs depend on highly complex architectures, resulting in computational costs that exceed the limits of mobile hardware. Moreover, constructing such sophisticated models requires aggregating extensive user data, which raises significant privacy concerns. Directly loading these models onto publicly accessible mobile devices exposes sensitive user information to substantial privacy risks. To address both the resource and privacy challenges of on-device deep learning, we introduce a private model compression approach. This method employs the knowledge distillation framework, integrating hint learning, distillation learning, and self learning techniques to develop a streamlined and efficient neural network. The knowledge transferred from the large teacher network is adaptively constrained and deliberately perturbed to fulfill differential privacy guarantees. Additionally, we develop a refined query sample selection strategy to minimize the number of queries and regulate privacy budget consumption. Comprehensive experiments alongside deployment on an Android device demonstrate that this approach not only achieves effective compression of large models but also ensures robust privacy protection. Specifically, on the SVHN dataset, under a significant (9.83,10^{-6})-differential privacy constraint, the resulting compact model attains a 20-fold compression and a 19-fold acceleration with only a 0.97% drop in accuracy.

author: Adams
title: An Empirical Examination of the Alleged Conflict Between Label Smoothing and Knowledge Distillation
abstract: In this study, we investigate the recently proposed claim that label smoothing conflicts with knowledge distillation from an empirical standpoint. Initially, we outline the reasoning behind this asserted incompatibility, specifically that label smoothing removes relative information contained within teacher logits. We then establish a new perspective on the impact of label smoothing on the distribution of classes with semantic similarity and dissimilarity. Subsequently, a quantitative metric is introduced to assess the extent of information loss in sample representations. Utilizing extensive analyses, visualizations, and a broad scope of experiments across Image Classification, Binary Networks, and Neural Machine Translation, we reveal limitations and the one-sided nature of this incompatibility assertion. We conclude by discussing conditions under which label smoothing genuinely fails to preserve its advantages.

author: Clark
title: Developing a Model-Agnostic Federated Learning Framework Utilizing Knowledge Distillation
abstract: Can we establish a universal interface enabling a spontaneous coalition of data holders (agents) to jointly execute federated learning? Such an interface must be independent of the agents’ model architectures, avoiding any assumptions about them, and cannot depend on access to representative public datasets. Utilizing knowledge distillation (KD) emerges as the natural strategy in crafting these protocols. Nonetheless, we reveal that many intuitive KD-based federated learning approaches exhibit subpar outcomes. To examine this phenomenon, we introduce a novel theoretical model, Federated Kernel ridge regression, that accounts for disparities in both model structure and data distribution. Our findings indicate that the primary cause of performance decline stems from an inherent limitation of KD when data heterogeneity is present. We corroborate this framework by evaluating and developing new KD-oriented protocols whose experimental results on neural networks with real datasets, though still inadequate, align closely with the theoretical expectations.

author: Hahn
title: A Universal Distillation Approach for Object Detectors Using Pearson Correlation Coefficient
abstract: Training lightweight models in object detection commonly employs knowledge distillation (KD). Despite its popularity, distillation between heterogeneous detectors remains underexplored. We experimentally demonstrate that superior FPN features extracted from a teacher detector with a different architecture can still benefit a student, even when their detection heads and label assignments vary. Nonetheless, straightforward feature map alignment for distillation encounters two main challenges. One is the feature magnitude discrepancy between teacher and student, which may impose excessively rigid constraints on the student network. The other issue is that certain FPN stages and channels possessing large magnitudes in the teacher can dominate the gradient of the distillation loss, thereby overshadowing contributions from other features and introducing notable noise. To mitigate these problems, we propose using Pearson Correlation Coefficient to imitate features, emphasizing relational information from the teacher while easing constraints on feature magnitude. This approach consistently surpasses existing KD methods for detection and is effective for both homogeneous and heterogeneous teacher-student configurations. Additionally, it accelerates convergence. Utilizing a strong MaskRCNN-Swin as the teacher, RetinaNet and FCOS powered by ResNet-50 achieve 41.5% and 43.9% mAP on COCO2017, corresponding to improvements of 4.1% and 4.8% over their respective baselines.

author: Walter
title: Distilling Knowledge Effectively from Teachers with Superior Performance
abstract: This work addresses knowledge distillation scenarios where the teacher models and training protocols represent advanced state-of-the-art benchmarks, contrasting with previous methods that concentrate on baseline conditions with relatively weaker teachers. Through empirical observation, we identify that prediction disparities between the student and a more capable teacher tend to be pronounced. Consequently, directly enforcing prediction alignment via KL divergence can hinder training and degrade the performance of standard approaches. We demonstrate that maintaining the relational structure among teacher and student predictions alone is sufficient, introducing a correlation-driven loss to explicitly encode the inherent inter-class associations derived from the teacher's outputs. Additionally, acknowledging the varying semantic proximities of instances to classes, this relational matching extends to intra-class similarities. The proposed technique is straightforward yet effective, showing robust adaptability across diverse model architectures, sizes, and training schemes. Comprehensive experiments reveal consistent state-of-the-art outcomes on image classification, object detection, and semantic segmentation benchmarks. The implementation can be found at: https://github.com/hunto/DIST_KD .

author: Edwards
title: Enhancing Privacy in Federated Learning via Ensemble-based Cross-Domain Offline Knowledge Distillation
abstract: Federated Learning (FL) enables collaborative training of a global model by local clients while keeping training data decentralized. Conventional FL approaches often rely on exchanging model parameters or utilize co-distillation strategies to manage imbalanced data distributions, yet these solutions face communication limitations and pose privacy risks. We introduce a communication-efficient and privacy-aware technique within the FL setting that performs a one-shot offline knowledge distillation utilizing unlabeled public datasets from different domains. Our approach constructs a quantized, noisy ensemble of predictions originating from fully trained local models to ensure stronger privacy guarantees without diminishing accuracy. Through comprehensive experiments on image and text classification benchmarks, we demonstrate that the proposed privacy-preserving strategy surpasses established FL baselines, achieving enhanced accuracy and communication efficiency.

author: Rios
title: Enhancing Neural Topic Modeling through Knowledge Distillation Techniques
abstract: Large collections of documents are often explored using topic models that yield patterns interpretable by humans. By employing knowledge distillation, we integrate the strengths of pretrained transformers with probabilistic topic modeling. The proposed approach is modular and can be readily combined with any neural topic model to boost the quality of topics. We validate this by applying it to two neural topic models with distinct architectures, achieving topic coherence that surpasses existing benchmarks. Additionally, our flexible framework not only enhances overall topic performance as usually measured but also excels in direct pairwise evaluations of corresponding topics.

author: Foster
title: Knowledge Distillation Employing Ensembles for CTR Prediction
abstract: Deep learning techniques have recently gained traction for enhancing click-through rate (CTR) prediction accuracy in various industrial settings. Most prior work emphasizes designing intricate network structures to model complex feature relationships and dynamic user interactions. Such complexity, however, often results in slower real-time inference, limiting practical deployment. Our study instead proposes a novel training approach leveraging knowledge distillation (KD), wherein a teacher-student framework transfers knowledge from a teacher to a simpler student model. This approach permits the student to be a basic DNN while still surpassing state-of-the-art teacher models in accuracy. Motivated by these gains, we extend the approach by incorporating an ensemble of teacher models to further improve student training precision. To support ensemble-based CTR prediction, we introduce innovative mechanisms including a gating function among teachers and early stopping criteria guided by distillation loss. Extensive evaluations on three industrial datasets comparing against 12 benchmark models demonstrate the advantages of the proposed KD method. Outcomes from both offline assessments and live A/B experiments validate the efficacy of this knowledge distillation training paradigm.

author: Rocha
title: Network Compression Using Limited Samples Through Layerwise Mutual Distillation
abstract: Compressing deep neural networks into smaller models is commonly used to create lightweight architectures. Most existing approaches depend on fine-tuning with ample labeled data to maintain accuracy, which may be hindered by concerns related to data privacy and security. Addressing this trade-off, we study network compression under few-shot conditions: given only a few examples per category, how can the network be compressed while incurring minimal degradation in performance? The key difficulty stems from substantial estimation errors during inference when relying on the original model, as compression tends to cause overfitting on sparse training samples. Such errors accumulate progressively across layers and ultimately impair the final output. To mitigate this issue, we introduce a novel layer-by-layer mutual knowledge transfer strategy, termed cross distillation, which couples intermediate representations of the teacher and student models to constrain error propagation. Our approach serves as a flexible framework compatible with mainstream compression techniques including pruning. Empirical results across standard benchmarks reveal that the proposed cross distillation mechanism markedly enhances the accuracy of the compressed student network under scenarios with limited training data.

author: Ellis
title: Investigating Representation-Based Knowledge Distillation Techniques for Graph Neural Networks
abstract: Utilizing knowledge distillation to enhance the efficiency of graph neural networks (GNNs) by leveraging more complex teacher models is a common approach. Previous research introduced the Local Structure Preserving (LSP) loss, aligning edge-defined local structural patterns between teacher and student node embeddings. This study examines the potential benefits of focusing on conserving the overall embedding topology derived from the teacher, given that real-world graphs may include hidden relationships and noisy connections. We propose a method based on contrastive learning, termed Graph Contrastive Representation Distillation (G-CRD), which implicitly conserves the global structure by bringing the student’s node embeddings closer to the teacher’s within a mutual representation space. Furthermore, we present a broader benchmark suite using large-scale, real-world datasets where noticeable performance differences exist between teacher and student GNNs. Our evaluation over four datasets and fourteen diverse GNN models demonstrates that the proposed method consistently enhances the accuracy and stability of lightweight GNNs, surpassing the original LSP, a global structure variant of LSP, and relevants baselines from two-dimensional computer vision. A deeper examination of the representational similarities between teacher and student spaces indicates that the method successfully balances local and global relational preservation, whereas structure-focused methods tend to emphasize one at the expense of the other. The implementation code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/chaitjo/efficient-gnns

author: Baker
title: Enhancing Low-Frequency Vocabulary Utilization: Optimizing Parallel Corpora in Non-Autoregressive Translation
abstract: Synthetic data generation through knowledge distillation (KD) is a common practice for training non-autoregressive translation (NAT) architectures. Despite its prevalence, a mismatch in low-frequency vocabulary between distilled and original datasets results in increased prediction errors on rare words. To address this, we incorporate raw corpora directly into NAT model training via pretraining techniques. An investigation of directed alignment patterns reveals that while KD enforces more deterministic alignments from low-frequency source terms to target tokens, it insufficiently aligns low-frequency words in the target back to the source. In response, we introduce a reverse knowledge distillation strategy aimed at revitalizing alignments for low-frequency target terms. Integrating these dual approaches to synergistically exploit both genuine and synthesized data yields a novel training paradigm that enhances NAT accuracy. Evaluations conducted across five language pairs using two state-of-the-art NAT architectures confirm that the proposed methodology substantially and consistently reduces errors in translating low-frequency words, improving overall translation quality. Notably, results on the WMT14 English-German and WMT16 Romanian-English benchmarks demonstrate BLEU scores of 28.2 and 33.9, respectively. Implementations, datasets, and trained models are accessible at the provided repository.

author: Wright
title: Semantic Distillation Integrated with Monocular Video for Holistic Scene Analysis
abstract: Autonomous systems require complete perception of their environment. It has been demonstrated that geometry (depth) and motion (optical flow) can be learned by deep neural networks from single-camera video data without relying on explicit ground truth labels, which are particularly scarce for these problems. Extending this capability, the present work simultaneously acquires depth, motion, and semantic information from monocular input, with semantic supervision acquired via a pre-trained model that provides distilled proxy ground truth images. Our approach tackles these three objectives simultaneously by employing (a) a newly designed training strategy combining knowledge distillation with self-supervision and (b) an efficient network architecture optimized for both high-performance GPUs and energy-constrained embedded devices. Extensive evaluation confirms that our method achieves leading performance across monocular depth prediction, optical flow, and motion segmentation benchmarks.

author: Hoffman
title: Knowledge Distillation in Federated Settings
abstract: In distributed training, sharing model parameters among participants is a common approach instead of directly transferring their original datasets. Federated learning exemplifies this by exchanging either gradients or network weights for each neural model. Nevertheless, when communication bandwidth is constrained, this strategy is inefficient, especially for modern deep networks that contain millions of parameters. Federated distillation (FD) emerges as an attractive alternative since it transfers only model predictions, whose dimensionality is generally much smaller than the full parameter space (for instance, the 10-label output in MNIST). This chapter aims to thoroughly elucidate FD, highlighting its advantages in reducing communication load and its versatility across tasks. Initially, the chapter presents a new asymptotic theoretical analysis based on neural tangent kernel (NTK) theory for two fundamental FD algorithms: knowledge distillation (KD) and co-distillation (CD). Subsequently, it discusses a foundational FD implementation focused on classification and compares its accuracy and communication demands against federated learning (FL). Finally, the chapter explores two specific case studies showcasing FD’s usability in diverse distributed learning scenarios: one addressing FD over asymmetric wireless channels with distinct uplink and downlink capacities, and another applying FD within reinforcement learning contexts.

author: Baker
title: Integrating Diverse Classifiers via a Distillation-Based Approach
abstract: We investigate the challenge of combining knowledge from multiple classifiers that vary in architecture and target categories into a single model using only a generic unlabelled dataset. Termed the problem of unifying heterogeneous classifiers, this task arises when data originates from different sources unable to share raw data—often due to privacy restrictions—permitting only model sharing. Furthermore, each individual source may lack data for all categories and differ in computational capacity, making uniform classifier training unfeasible. To address this, we extend knowledge distillation to accommodate heterogeneous classifiers. By formulating a probabilistic link between classifier outputs and the full class probability distribution, we introduce two methodological frameworks: one utilizing cross-entropy minimization and another employing matrix factorization. Both methods enable estimation of soft labels across all classes from unlabelled data, replacing ground truth for training a consolidated classifier. Comprehensive experiments conducted on ImageNet, LSUN, and Places365 datasets demonstrate that our methods markedly surpass straightforward distillation extensions and approach the accuracy levels of classifiers trained in a centralized supervised fashion.

author: Richards
title: Text Generation Leveraging Knowledge Distillation Combined with Generative Adversarial Networks
abstract: The generation of text plays a crucial role in various NLP tasks including language modeling, text summarization, and machine translation. While generative adversarial networks (GANs) have demonstrated outstanding capabilities in producing high-quality images within computer vision, their adoption in NLP has recently attracted considerable attention despite challenges arising from text's discrete structure. This study proposes a knowledge distillation technique designed to harness GAN architectures effectively for text generation. We illustrate that autoencoders (AEs) enable the creation of continuous sentence representations, which are smooth and assign positive probabilities across multiple words. By distilling these continuous representations, the generator is trained to produce analogous smooth outputs. Extensive experiments conducted on multiple datasets validate our approach, indicating superior results measured by BLEU scores and Jensen-Shannon distance (JSD) compared to conventional GAN-based text generation methods that lack pre-training.

author: Hurst
title: Effective Training of Compact Ranking Models for Recommender Systems via Knowledge Transfer
abstract: This work introduces a distinctive training approach aimed at generating ranking models for recommender systems that maintain high accuracy alongside computational efficiency. Inspired by the success of knowledge distillation (KD) in image classification, we adapt KD to ranking challenges with a method referred to here as ranking distillation. In this setup, a compact student model simultaneously learns from the original training data and guidance provided by a larger, more complex teacher model. The resultant student maintains ranking accuracy close to the teacher's while benefiting from reduced size, which enhances inference speed during deployment. The proposed method demonstrates versatility, as it can be combined with various architectures chosen for both teacher and student ranking models. We detail how ranking distillation overcomes specific hurdles associated with ranking tasks. Evaluations performed on publicly available datasets employing leading recommendation frameworks confirm that the student model trained with this approach retains ranking effectiveness comparable to the teacher, requires less than half the memory of the teacher, and significantly outperforms the student trained without knowledge distillation.

author: Ross
title: Distilling Ensembles into Single Models for Neural Machine Translation
abstract: A technique known as knowledge distillation enables the training of a student network with enhanced performance by leveraging a more powerful teacher network. Neural Machine Translation (NMT) inference demands considerable computation time, which can be mitigated by employing a more compact model. We illustrate a procedure to compress the translation performance of both an ensemble and an oracle BLEU-calibrated teacher into a single NMT architecture. Additionally, we report gains achieved when the teacher network shares the same structure and size as the student. Given the costly nature of student model training, we propose a training data selection strategy guided by teacher knowledge that accelerates training while simultaneously enhancing translation accuracy. Our approach requires no modifications to the codebase and is straightforward to apply to any NMT model, thereby reducing inference latency.

author: Robinson
title: Analyzing and Enhancing Lexical Selection in Non-Autoregressive Translation Models
abstract: Non-autoregressive translation (NAT) models rely heavily on knowledge distillation (KD) that simplifies raw data through an autoregressive teacher model during training. In this work, we demonstrate empirically that lexical choice mistakes concerning infrequent words tend to be transferred from the teacher to the NAT model as an unintended consequence of this process. To mitigate these errors, we propose incorporating the original raw data during NAT training to recover valuable information related to low-frequency words that distillation typically omits. Specifically, we add a supplementary Kullback-Leibler divergence loss based on the comparison between the lexical choices made by the NAT model and those present in the raw data. Experiments performed on multiple language pairs and architectures confirm the proposed method’s effectiveness and broad applicability. In-depth analyses verify that performance gains arise primarily from a reduction in lexical choice errors affecting rare words. Importantly, our approach achieves state-of-the-art NAT results on the WMT14 English-German and WMT16 Romanian-English benchmarks, attaining 27.8 and 33.8 BLEU scores, respectively. Code implementation will be made publicly available.

author: Bright
title: Efficient and Distilled Modeling Approaches for Practical Lipreading Applications
abstract: The advancement of lipreading capabilities has been largely driven by renewed interest in neural network techniques. While earlier studies have concentrated on maximizing accuracy through architectural optimization and enhancing generalization, practical deployment requirements remain unmet by existing methods. This research introduces multiple contributions aimed at closing this divide: initially, employing self-distillation elevates top performance substantially on the LRW and LRW-1000 datasets, achieving 88.5% and 46.6% accuracy respectively. Subsequently, we integrate new architectural modifications, prominently featuring a Depthwise Separable Temporal Convolutional Network (DS-TCN) head, which drastically reduces computational demands compared to the already computationally modest baseline. Furthermore, knowledge distillation proves critical for regaining predictive capacity in these compact architectures. The outcome is a suite of models presenting diverse balances between accuracy and efficiency. Notably, the leading lightweight models achieve performance comparable to leading techniques in the field while decreasing computational load and parameter count by factors of 8.2 and 3.9, respectively. This advancement is anticipated to facilitate the practical use of lipreading systems.

author: Hicks
title: Adapting Knowledge for Domain Transfer in Machine Learning
abstract: In numerous practical applications, domain adaptation plays a vital role when training and testing data follow different distributions. Conventional deep learning methods addressing domain adaptation require simultaneous training on both source and target domain datasets. This constraint limits their usefulness in contexts involving many domains or dynamically changing domains, such as spam detection, where adversaries frequently alter their strategies. To address these limitations, we introduce an approach extending knowledge distillation techniques to domain adaptation. Our method employs multiple teacher models representing different source domains and leverages the relationships among these domains to guide a student model. We demonstrate that this approach attains top-tier results on unsupervised multi-source domain adaptation using a well-known sentiment analysis dataset. For scenarios involving only a single teacher, reliance solely on domain similarity as an indicator of the teacher’s reliability proves insufficient. Therefore, we develop a straightforward metric that reliably predicts the teacher's accuracy within the target domain. Utilizing examples identified with high confidence by this metric, the student model achieves state-of-the-art outcomes in single-source adaptation tasks.

author: Williams
title: Data-Free Knowledge Distillation Through Adversarial Alignment of Beliefs
abstract: Transferring knowledge from a large teacher model to a more compact student network is a common practice in current deep learning. Yet, access to the original training data is often restricted due to escalating dataset scales and privacy constraints. We introduce an approach where a student network learns to replicate the teacher's output distributions entirely without access to either the training data or any ancillary information. This is accomplished by employing an adversarial generator that synthesizes input images on which the student’s predictions diverge most from the teacher’s, subsequently leveraging these samples to enhance the student’s performance. Our technique yields a student that effectively mimics the teacher on straightforward datasets such as SVHN, and notably surpasses existing few-shot distillation results on CIFAR10 using only 100 examples per class, despite operating in a data-free manner. Additionally, we define a novel metric to assess belief alignment near decision boundaries, revealing that our zero-shot student demonstrates a significantly tighter match to the teacher than a student trained with actual data. The implementation is publicly accessible at: https://github.com/polo5/ZeroShotKnowledgeTransfer

author: Rodriguez
title: A Knowledge Distillation Approach to Capture and Extend Insights from Graph Neural Networks
abstract: Graph-based semi-supervised classification remains a critical challenge within machine learning. Contemporary graph neural network (GNN) architectures have demonstrated significant performance gains compared to classical approaches like label propagation. Nevertheless, these sophisticated GNNs involve complex prediction functions that may not fully exploit intrinsic domain knowledge—for instance, the tendency of nodes with structural relationships to share class labels. To tackle this, we introduce a knowledge distillation framework that transfers learned representations from any pre-trained GNN teacher model into a specially constructed student network. This student combines two straightforward predictive components: label propagation and feature transformation, thereby inherently capturing structure-driven and feature-driven priors. Specifically, the student model is formulated as a trainable integration of parameterized modules corresponding to these two mechanisms. Consequently, the distilled student assimilates both the teacher’s knowledge and prior structural and feature information for enhanced prediction capabilities. Additionally, this approach yields a student model with a prediction process that is more interpretable than the original GNNs. Extensive evaluation across five standard public benchmarks using seven diverse GNN teacher models—including GCN, GAT, APPNP, SAGE, SGC, GCNII, and GLP—demonstrates that the student model consistently surpasses each respective teacher by a margin ranging from 1.4% to 4.7% on average. The full implementation and datasets are accessible at https://github.com/BUPT-GAMMA/CPF.

author: Burton
title: Hardware-Compatible Block Structured Pruning for Scalable Transformer-based Language Model Compression
abstract: Large-scale language models pre-trained for natural language processing tasks have shown outstanding accuracy. Nonetheless, their adoption is hindered by the constraints of limited memory capacity and processing speed on hardware, posing challenges particularly in edge computing environments. This study introduces a transformer-based large-scale language representation optimized through hardware-compatible block-structured pruning. Optimization is carried out by integrating reweighted group Lasso within the block-structured pruning framework. Beyond substantial reductions in both weight storage and computational demand, the approach attains elevated compression ratios. Evaluations on BERT, RoBERTa, and DistilBERT across the General Language Understanding Evaluation (GLUE) tasks reveal compression rates reaching up to 5.0x with negligible or no loss in accuracy on specific tasks. Furthermore, this technique complements existing compact pre-trained models such as DistilBERT derived via knowledge distillation, enabling an additional average compression factor of 1.79x with minimal or absent accuracy loss. This method facilitates deployment of compressed models on devices with stringent resource limitations.

author: Conner
title: Extracting Task-Relevant Information from BERT to Train Lightweight Neural Models
abstract: Within natural language processing, the trend toward increasingly deep and complex neural architectures continues, exemplified by models like BERT, ELMo, and GPT. This progression has fostered the view that earlier, shallower neural models for language comprehension have become outdated. Contrarily, we illustrate that simple, efficient neural networks remain competitive without modifying their architecture, incorporating external datasets, or utilizing extra input features. Our approach transfers knowledge from the state-of-the-art BERT model into a single-layer BiLSTM and its siamese variant for tasks involving sentence pairs. Evaluations across various datasets covering paraphrasing, natural language inference, and sentiment analysis yield performance on par with ELMo, while requiring approximately 100 times fewer parameters and achieving inference speeds roughly 15 times faster.

author: Henderson
title: Enhancing MLPs with Knowledge Distillation from GNNs for Graph-Free Neural Inference
abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) excel in graph-based node classification but face scalability limitations in industrial scenarios due to their reliance on multi-hop neighbor data, which increases latency in time-sensitive applications. While techniques such as pruning and quantization reduce the number of Multiplication-and-ACcumulation (MAC) operations to accelerate GNN inference, these do not fully overcome the data dependency bottleneck. Multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs), in contrast, operate without graph-based input dependencies and thus offer much faster inference times, albeit generally at the cost of lower node classification accuracy compared to GNNs. Inspired by the complementary aspects of GNNs and MLPs, the proposed method applies knowledge distillation (KD) from GNN teachers to MLP students, substantially boosting MLP classification performance. These distilled MLP models, which eliminate graph dependency during inference, are defined as graph-free neural networks. The graph-free neural networks demonstrate inference speedups ranging from 146X to 273X relative to GNNs, and 14X to 27X compared to existing GNN acceleration methodologies, while maintaining competitive accuracy. Experiments covering both transductive and inductive setups across seven benchmark datasets reveal that the distilled MLPs improve accuracy by an average of 12.36% compared to standalone MLPs and achieve parity with GNN results on six out of seven datasets. Detailed investigation identifies conditions that enable such parity with GNNs and underlines the potential of graph-free neural networks as an effective solution for latency-sensitive environments.

author: Brown
title: A Comprehensive Framework for Compression of Vision Transformers
abstract: Recently, vision transformers (ViTs) have become widely adopted. Without employing specialized image processing operations such as convolutions, these ViTs manage to achieve competitive results when trained on extremely large datasets. Nevertheless, their computational cost remains a significant challenge, primarily due to stacking multiple multi-head self-attention layers and related components. Although extensive work exists on compression methods for convolutional neural networks, studies focusing on compressing Vision Transformers are more nascent, typically addressing one or two compression strategies in isolation. In this work, we introduce an integrated ViT compression framework that jointly incorporates three powerful methods: pruning, layer skipping, and knowledge distillation. We cast the problem as an end-to-end optimization task constrained by a computational budget, simultaneously learning the model’s weights, pruning ratios and masks for each layer, as well as skip configurations, all under the guidance of a distillation objective. This optimization is solved via the primal-dual approach. Evaluations performed on multiple ViT variants including DeiT and T2T-ViT backbones using the ImageNet dataset demonstrate that our method consistently surpasses recent state-of-the-art approaches. Specifically, the DeiT-Tiny model can be reduced to approximately 50% of its original FLOPs with minimal accuracy degradation. The implementation is publicly accessible at the provided URL.

author: James
title: Progressive Self-Distillation for Enhanced Robustness in Cross-Modal Representation Learning
abstract: CLIP's vision-language training objective struggles to handle the noisy many-to-many relationships inherent in image caption datasets gathered from the web, leading to inefficiencies in computation and data usage. To overcome this issue, we propose a new training methodology utilizing cross-modal contrastive learning combined with progressive self-distillation and soft alignments between images and text, to effectively acquire stable representations despite noisy inputs. Within each minibatch, our model refines its parameters by self-distilling knowledge to produce soft-alignment targets for selected image-caption pairs. Comprehensive testing on 14 benchmark datasets demonstrates consistent superiority over the original CLIP model across various tasks: zero-shot classification, linear probe transfer, and image-text retrieval, all achieved without increasing computational demands. Further investigation employing an ImageNet-derived robustness evaluation framework indicates that our approach attains improved effective robustness against natural shifts in data distribution compared to both models trained on ImageNet and CLIP itself. Finally, experiments on pretraining datasets ranging over two orders of magnitude in size reveal that performance gains relative to CLIP are positively correlated with the amount of training data.

author: Ferrell
title: Enhanced Supernet Optimization through Adaptive Alpha-Divergence in Neural Architecture Search
abstract: Neural architecture search (NAS) utilizing weight-sharing is a powerful method for automatic design of efficient architectures. This approach constructs a supernet encompassing all candidate architectures as its subnetworks, training them together. The performance of weight-sharing NAS critically depends on the effective knowledge transfer from the supernet (teacher) to its subnetworks (students). Commonly employed KL divergence for distillation can cause subnetworks to either overestimate or underestimate the teacher supernet’s uncertainty, degrading their effectiveness. In this study, we introduce training of the supernet employing a generalized alpha-divergence, adaptively chosen to balance the bias in uncertainty estimation of the teacher. We integrate this alpha-divergence based objective into training regimes for both slimmable networks and weight-sharing NAS, observing substantial performance gains. Our experimental results reveal that the model family identified using this method surpasses established benchmarks such as BigNAS, Once-for-All, and AttentiveNAS across diverse FLOPs constraints. Notably, we report an ImageNet top-1 accuracy of 80.0% at a computational cost of 444M FLOPs. The implementation and pretrained weights are accessible at https://github.com/facebookresearch/AlphaNet.

author: Rice
title: Improving Generalization in Fake Media Identification through Sequential Representation Learning Combined with Distillation
abstract: Artificial intelligence has advanced substantially during recent decades, yet it continues to depend largely on static datasets within non-changing environments. A developing research area, continual learning, explores how AI models may acquire knowledge incrementally from an ongoing succession of correlated inputs, mimicking biological learning processes. Concurrently, the rise of synthesized media, including deepfakes and GAN-produced face images, has posed notable challenges for multimedia applications. Although various techniques have been introduced recently that detect deepfakes with notable precision, their performance is often limited by dependence on static datasets and narrow evaluation scenarios. To address this, our study integrates continual learning principles into neural network training dynamics, focusing on significant improvements in data utilization efficiency. We introduce a method that merges the principles of continual learning, representation learning, and knowledge distillation, termed here as the proposed method. This framework is crafted to sequentially adapt to new domains represented by deepfake and GAN-synthesized face datasets, while effectively mitigating catastrophic forgetting within a teacher-student paradigm. Comprehensive experimental evidence highlights that our proposed approach excels in adapting to diverse domains for identifying low-quality deepfake videos and images generated by GANs across multiple datasets, surpassing existing state-of-the-art techniques.

author: Maddox
title: Layerwise Distillation Utilizing Earth Mover's Distance for BERT Model Size Reduction via Many-to-Many Correspondences
abstract: Large-scale pre-trained language models such as BERT have demonstrated outstanding outcomes across a variety of natural language processing (NLP) benchmarks. The challenge remains that their substantial storage requirements and computational demands limit practical application on hardware with restricted resources. To address this, we introduce a new distillation technique for BERT that employs many-to-many layer correspondence, enabling every student network layer within the intermediate range to assimilate knowledge from any intermediate teacher layer. This flexibility allows the student to adaptively capture information pertinent to distinct NLP tasks. Complementing this, we incorporate Earth Mover's Distance (EMD) to quantify the minimum accumulated cost required to transfer knowledge between the teacher and student architectures. EMD facilitates an effective alignment for the many-to-many layer correspondences, even when layer sizes differ. Additionally, we design a cost attention framework to automatically assign weights to layers during EMD computation, aiming to enhance the distillation quality and expedite training convergence. Comprehensive evaluations on the GLUE benchmark reveal that our approach delivers results on par with advanced baselines, both in accuracy and compression efficiency.

author: Valencia
title: A Review of Deep Learning Model Compression Techniques for Text Applications
abstract: Significant advancements in natural language processing (NLP) and information retrieval (IR) have been driven by deep learning architectures such as Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), Gated Recurrent Units (GRUs), Long Short-Term Memory (LSTMs) networks, and Transformer-based models including Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT), Generative Pre-training Transformer (GPT-2), Multi-task Deep Neural Network (MT-DNN), Extra-Long Network (XLNet), Text-to-text transfer transformer (T5), T-NLG, and GShard. However, these models typically possess very large sizes. Conversely, practical deployments require models with reduced size, decreased latency, and minimized computational energy consumption. This review covers six categories of methods—Pruning, Quantization, Knowledge Distillation, Parameter Sharing, Tensor Decomposition, and Sub-quadratic Transformer architectures—that focus on compressing such models to facilitate their use in industrial NLP systems. Considering the pressing demand for compact and efficient models, alongside the substantial research output recently emerging, this survey consolidates the extensive contributions from the deep learning community in NLP over recent years into a unified narrative.

author: Smith
title: Neural Architecture Search for Efficient Generative Adversarial Network Compression
abstract: The increasing necessity to deploy Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) on mobile platforms for diverse tasks including image translation, enhancement, and editing has stimulated interest in GAN model compression. Despite extensive progress in compressing other deep architectures, the area of GAN compression—particularly of generators—remains underexplored. Current techniques for GAN compression often cater to specific architectures and loss functions. Motivated by the advancements in AutoML-driven model compression, we propose leveraging AutoML to compress GANs by developing a novel automated distillation framework. Our approach initiates with a carefully constructed search space specialized for efficient generator design. It conducts an end-to-end search to identify compact generators aligned with predefined computational budgets. This search process is guided by knowledge distillation from the original GAN generator, enabling effective compression. The method operates fully autonomously, does not require pretrained discriminators, and is broadly applicable across GAN architectures. We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach on two exemplar GAN tasks: image translation and super resolution. The resulting compressed models are substantially lighter while achieving more competitive performance compared to existing methods, even without additional enhancement techniques. The implementation and pretrained weights are publicly accessible at https://github.com/TAMU-VITA/AGD.

author: Le
title: Enhancing Video-Pose Representations for Activity of Daily Living Recognition
abstract: Recognizing Activities of Daily Living (ADL) frequently involves merging RGB data with 3D poses, as ADL activities often appear alike and require detailed modeling to correctly differentiate them. Since contemporary 3D ConvNets lack flexibility in capturing subtle action-specific visual cues, the predominant methodologies incorporate both RGB and 3D Pose information. However, generating 3D poses from RGB inputs entails considerable computational expense when dedicated sensors are absent, restricting the practical deployment of these methods in latency-sensitive contexts. Addressing this challenge, we introduce an augmented pose-driven attention framework: the proposed method extends the earlier Video-Pose Network (VPN) by investigating two pathways—first, by distilling pose information into RGB representations at the feature level, and second, by emulating pose-guided attention through attention-level distillation. These strategies are combined within a unified architecture, termed VPN++. We demonstrate that VPN++ not only achieves strong performance but also offers substantial acceleration and robustness against noisy pose inputs. Across four public datasets, VPN++ surpasses established benchmarks both with and without the availability of 3D poses. Code is accessible at https://github.com/srijandas07/vpnplusplus.

author: Maldonado
title: Transferring Knowledge via Emulation of Intermediate Representations
abstract: Using knowledge distillation (KD) to train compact student networks guided by larger teacher networks is a well-established approach. Whereas conventional KD techniques rely on the teacher's softened output logits to supervise the student, we propose that encouraging the student to replicate features from the teacher's penultimate layer provides a superior advantage. This strategy enables direct transfer of richer information and applies to teacher networks that do not utilize a softmax output. Empirical results demonstrate that this feature replication surpasses the accuracy levels of traditional KD. To enhance this approach, we separate feature representations into magnitude and direction components, positing that the student should have flexibility in magnitude while focusing on faithfully reproducing feature directions. Accordingly, we introduce a loss function derived from locality-sensitive hashing (LSH) that prioritizes directional similarity. This novel loss enables improved alignment of feature directions, alleviates constraints on feature magnitudes, and leads to top-tier distillation performance. We furnish theoretical justification for how LSH supports directional feature replication and extend the framework to encompass tasks such as multi-label classification and object detection.

author: Herrera
title: Reducing GAN Size via Knowledge Distillation Techniques
abstract: Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) serve numerous machine learning objectives, including domain adaptation, enhancing image resolution, and producing synthetic datasets. Leading GAN architectures typically contain tens of millions of parameters, limiting their viability for deployment in environments with constraints on size, weight, and power (SWAP), such as on mobile platforms or in real-time scenarios. To date, no prior studies explicitly address minimizing the parameter count in GANs. We introduce a compression approach utilizing knowledge distillation, where a more compact "student" GAN is trained to replicate the behavior of a significantly larger "teacher" GAN. Applying this distillation procedure to MNIST, CIFAR-10, and Celeb-A datasets yields compression ratios of 1669:1, 58:1, and 87:1, respectively, while maintaining the generative image quality. Our experimental results reveal an inherent qualitative threshold for compressing GANs effectively. Additionally, given an identical parameter constraint, the compressed GANs demonstrate superior performance compared to GANs trained with conventional methods. We hypothesize that this advantage stems partly from the optimization landscape characteristic of over-parameterized GANs, which facilitates effective training via alternating gradient descent. Consequently, training an over-parameterized GAN followed by our compression approach leads to a compact yet high-quality generative model.

author: Davidson
title: Enhancing Robustness in Re-Identification via Knowledge Distillation from Multiple Perspectives
abstract: Conventional techniques for achieving robustness in Re-Identification predominantly exploit tracking cues through a Video-To-Video framework. Yet, these approaches suffer notable performance degradation when applied to single image queries, such as in the Image-To-Video scenario. To overcome this limitation, recent research has concentrated on transferring temporal features learned by Video-based architectures to Image-based counterparts. In this study, we introduce a training paradigm that facilitates the transfer of richer knowledge derived from multiple viewpoints of the target entity. The proposed method employs a teacher-student learning scheme where the teacher utilizes a diverse set of views to guide a student exposed to fewer perspectives, utilizing the multiplicity of views as a supervisory signal. Consequently, the student model surpasses the teaching model and outperforms existing best Image-To-Video methods substantially, achieving improvements of 6.3% mAP on MARS, 8.6% on Duke-Video-ReID, and 5% on VeRi-776. We conduct an extensive evaluation spanning Person, Vehicle, and Animal Re-Identification tasks, offering both quantitative metrics and qualitative insights into the characteristics of the technique. The implementation code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/aimagelab/VKD.

author: Rodriguez
title: Differentially Private Release of Graph Neural Network Models
abstract: Graph neural networks (GNNs) have seen widespread adoption in domains involving sensitive information such as healthcare, raising significant privacy concerns regarding the trained models. Notably, even black-box access to a trained GNN can expose it to privacy threats including membership inference attacks. In this work, we develop a privacy-preserving framework to enable the release of GNN models under differential privacy in a centralized context. Our method operates under the assumption that a public unlabeled graph is accessible, allowing the training of GNN models using public data augmented with extracted knowledge from private data while maintaining privacy protections. This approach integrates knowledge distillation with two noise injection mechanisms—random subsampling and noisy labeling—to provide formal privacy guarantees. We conduct a theoretical evaluation within the Renyi differential privacy framework and demonstrate through empirical experiments that our technique achieves competitive results relative to multiple baselines adapted for graph data. The implementation code can be found at https://github.com/iyempissy/privGnn.

author: Graham
title: Federated Learning with Hierarchical Auxiliary Branches for Regularization
abstract: Data heterogeneity and client imbalance present substantial challenges in federated learning, often causing discrepancies among the local networks and hindering the stable convergence of the global model. To address these issues, we introduce a new architectural regularization approach that integrates multiple auxiliary branches within each local network by combining local and global subnetworks at various levels. This method enforces alignment of the main pathway’s representations in the local model with those of the auxiliary composite branches through online knowledge distillation. Our approach enhances the robustness of the global model under non-iid data distributions and is easily incorporated into diverse federated learning frameworks without increasing communication overhead. Extensive experiments validate significant improvements in accuracy and computational efficiency compared to prior approaches. The implementation is accessible on our project website.

author: Chavez
title: Knowledge Distillation of Deep Neural Networks Without Access to Original Data
abstract: Model compression techniques have recently demonstrated the ability to reduce the size of large neural network models considerably while largely preserving their accuracy. Nonetheless, these methods typically require availability of the original training data, which is not always feasible when the model was trained on massive datasets or on data with privacy or security restrictions, such as in biometric applications. We introduce a data-free knowledge distillation approach that compresses deep neural networks trained on extensive datasets to a smaller size using only additional metadata accompanying the pretrained model. Various types of metadata suitable for our approach are investigated, along with a discussion of the respective compromises in employing each.

author: Mckay
title: Efficient Large-scale Language Model Distillation via a Mixup-based Framework
abstract: Recent advances in large-scale language models exhibit strong empirical results, yet these improvements come at the expense of larger architectures, increased energy usage, and slower inference speeds, limiting deployment on resource-constrained devices. Knowledge distillation (KD) has proven to be a promising compression technique for these expansive models. Nevertheless, such large neural systems often memorize their training data and exhibit unstable prediction behaviors when slight shifts occur in the input distribution. Additionally, when task-specific datasets are scarce, students encounter limited chances to acquire beneficial knowledge from their teachers. To mitigate these challenges, we introduce a data-agnostic distillation methodology that incorporates mixup—a straightforward and effective data augmentation strategy—to foster enhanced generalization in the student model. Specifically, beyond matching teacher outputs on original samples, the student is trained to replicate the teacher’s responses on inputs formed by linear interpolations between pairs of examples. From a theoretical standpoint, we establish that under plausible assumptions, this approach reduces the discrepancy between generalization and empirical errors. Empirical evaluation on the GLUE benchmark confirms that this technique consistently surpasses typical KD and several strong alternative methods. Additional experimentation in settings with constrained data and ablations further highlights the benefits of the proposed method.

author: Liu
title: Facilitating Multimodal Output in CLIP Through Vision-Language Knowledge Transfer
abstract: Dual-stream architectures like CLIP that undergo extensive vision-language pre-training (VLP) on large-scale image-text pairs have demonstrated excellence in achieving multimodal alignment. However, these models lack effectiveness in multimodal generative tasks because of limitations in their text encoder. Addressing this, we introduce enhancement of the dual-stream VLP framework by integrating a pre-trained language model (PLM) focused on text via vision-language knowledge distillation (VLKD), thereby equipping the framework with multimodal generative capabilities. This approach, VLKD, demands considerably less data and computational resources when contrasted with training from the ground up. Our experiments exhibit that the enhanced model delivers robust zero-shot outcomes on tasks involving multimodal generation, including open-ended visual question answering and image captioning. Notably, it attains 44.5% zero-shot accuracy on the VQAv2 benchmark, outperforming the former leading zero-shot model while utilizing approximately seven times fewer parameters. Moreover, the innate textual language understanding and generative functions of the PLM remain intact following VLKD, ensuring the model's adaptability for both multimodal and unimodal applications.

author: Mason
title: Distilling Knowledge Through Feature Embedding in Student Networks
abstract: Convolutional neural networks with deep architectures have found extensive use across various domains; however, their high demand for memory and computational power limits their deployment on mobile platforms. The objective of knowledge distillation is to enhance a compact student model by transferring information from a pre-trained complex teacher model. Conventional approaches relying on teacher-student frameworks often incorporate extra fully connected layers to align intermediate representations, which significantly increases parameter count. This study instead focuses on transferring knowledge without introducing additional parameters requiring optimization. Viewing the teacher-student relationship through the lens of feature embedding, we apply a locality preserving loss that encourages the student to produce low-dimensional features retaining the essential characteristics present in the teacher's high-dimensional representations. Consequently, the distilled student model preserves performance comparable to the teacher model. A theoretical assessment confirms the lower computational complexity achieved by the proposed approach. Empirical evaluations on standard datasets and pretrained models demonstrate the method's superiority over existing teacher-student paradigms regarding both computational efficiency and storage requirements.

author: White
title: Compressing Generative Adversarial Networks for Efficient Image-to-Image Translation
abstract: Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have demonstrated success in diverse image-to-image translation applications, yet their intensive computational and storage demands restrict deployment on mobile platforms. While conventional network compression techniques typically target visual recognition problems, they rarely address generation tasks. Leveraging the concept of knowledge distillation, we train a student generator with a reduced number of parameters by transferring both low-level and high-level representations from a larger, pre-trained teacher generator. To enhance the student generator’s effectiveness, a dedicated student discriminator is introduced, which evaluates the differences among authentic images and those produced by both student and teacher generators. This setup leads to an adversarial training scheme that jointly optimizes the student generator and student discriminator. Experiments conducted on standard benchmark datasets provide both qualitative and quantitative evidence that the proposed compression strategy yields compact generative models maintaining strong performance.

author: Gaines
title: Task-Specific Compression of BERT via Differentiable Neural Architecture Search
abstract: Pre-trained language models like BERT have proven highly effective in a wide array of natural language processing tasks. Nonetheless, their substantial parameter count poses challenges for deployment in real-time settings that necessitate rapid inference with constrained computational resources. Current BERT compression approaches generate smaller models but do so without tailoring to individual downstream tasks, applying a universal compressed model across all tasks. Addressing the need for task-focused BERT compression, we introduce a compression technique that employs differentiable Neural Architecture Search to derive compact BERT variants customized to each specific task. This approach uses a task-specific knowledge distillation loss to guide the architecture search and incorporates an efficiency-aware loss as a constraint, balancing model effectiveness with resource efficiency in the task-adaptive compression process. Experiments across multiple NLP benchmarks show the resulting task-adaptive compressed models accelerate inference by factors ranging from 12.7x to 29.3x compared to the original BERT and reduce parameter counts by 11.5x to 17.0x, while maintaining comparable performance.

author: Harrell
title: Ensuring Participation of All Clients: Federated Learning Adapted for Devices with Varying Capabilities
abstract: Federated learning (FL) provides a critical approach for training centralized models using decentralized data while preserving privacy. Most existing FL approaches presuppose that any client can train the unified global model. Nonetheless, practical scenarios involve clients with heterogeneous devices possessing diverse computational strengths. Large-scale models such as BERT, despite their success in AI, pose challenges for deployment in heterogeneous FL environments involving resource-limited clients. Naive strategies like excluding underpowered clients or applying a uniformly small model result in drawbacks, including neglected contributions from excluded clients and decreased accuracy caused by data omission or insufficient model complexity. To address these issues, we introduce the proposed method, a client-inclusive federated learning technique that adapts to device heterogeneity. The central concept is allocating models of varying sizes matching each client's computational capability—larger models for robust clients, smaller ones for weaker devices. Additionally, we develop an effective mechanism to facilitate knowledge sharing across diverse local models of differing scale, enabling every client to engage in model training and ensuring the final aggregated model remains sufficiently large and capable. Moreover, we present a momentum knowledge distillation approach to enhance knowledge transfer from the larger models on high-capacity clients to the smaller models on the less capable ones. Comprehensive evaluations on multiple real-world benchmark datasets validate the proposed method’s superiority in training accurate models across heterogeneous client devices within the federated learning setting.

author: Evans
title: Training Efficient Metrics for Machine Translation
abstract: Advances in multilingual text generation and machine translation have prompted the use of learned evaluation metrics like COMET and BLEURT, which frame scoring as a regression task utilizing embeddings from multilingual pre-trained models including XLM-RoBERTa and mBERT. However, investigations on analogous problems indicate that larger model sizes tend to produce more effective results, though this comes with increased cost and evaluation impracticality. This work explores how model capacity interacts with multilingual capabilities by experimenting with RemBERT, a leading multilingual model, using data sourced from the WMT Metrics Shared Task. Through a sequence of studies, we confirm that the size of the model constitutes a limiting factor for cross-lingual generalization, and subsequently show that distillation techniques can mitigate this issue. Our approach combines synthetic data creation with knowledge transfer from a single teacher to multiple student models trained on linguistically related languages. Employing this strategy yields an improvement of up to 10.5% over standard fine-tuning and achieves 92.6% of the full RemBERT model’s effectiveness while utilizing only approximately one third of its parameter count.

author: Fowler
title: Self-supervised Knowledge Transfer for Compact Visual Models
abstract: Focusing on small models in self-supervised learning, this work is motivated by empirical evidence indicating that prevalent contrastive self-supervised approaches, while effective for large networks, underperform when applied to smaller architectures. To tackle this issue, a novel framework is presented that employs a larger model in the role of a teacher to impart representational information to a smaller student model through self-supervision. Rather than learning directly from unlabeled samples, the student encoder is optimized to replicate the similarity score distribution produced by the teacher network across a collection of data points. Experimental results demonstrate that this strategy substantially elevates the accuracy of small-scale networks on downstream benchmarks. Specifically, relative to existing self-supervised techniques, top-1 accuracy is enhanced from 42.2% to 67.6% on EfficientNet-B0 and from 36.3% to 68.2% on MobileNet-v3-Large using the ImageNet-1k dataset.

author: Lynch
title: Knowledge Distillation Across Modalities for Sensor-Based Action Recognition from Visual Inputs
abstract: Recent advances in human activity recognition (HAR) highlight improvements achieved through multi-modal data integration. Nonetheless, wearable platforms like smartwatches suffer from limited computational capabilities, hindering the direct application of these complex techniques. To address this limitation, we propose an end-to-end framework that distills knowledge from vision to sensor modalities. This approach requires solely time-series input, specifically accelerometer signals, during device inference, thereby alleviating computational burdens on edge hardware while approximating the accuracy of the resource-intensive multi-modal strategies. To better preserve temporal dependencies and support convolutional visual networks, we transform the time-series into two-dimensional representations utilizing the Gramian Angular Field encoding. Our experimental setup employs ResNet18 as the teacher and a multi-scale Temporal Relation Network with BN-Inception as the student. We introduce a specially designed loss termed Distance and Angle-wised Semantic Knowledge loss (DASK) to address discrepancies between visual and sensor data distributions. The proposed method's performance is rigorously validated on UTD-MHAD, MMAct, and Berkeley-MHAD datasets, showcasing its efficacy and suitability for deployment on wearable devices.

author: Hernandez
title: Converting Neural Radiance Fields into Neural Light Fields via Distillation for Rapid Novel View Rendering
abstract: Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) methods have recently demonstrated promising abilities to encode intricate scenes through neural representations. A significant limitation of NeRF lies in its slow inference speed, as synthesizing a single pixel necessitates hundreds of network evaluations. Prior approaches have largely focused on reducing the quantity of samples needed, yet the iterative sampling framework remains a bottleneck. Conversely, Neural Light Field (NeLF) offers a more direct formulation for novel view synthesis where rendering each pixel involves only a single forward pass without ray-marching computations. In this study, we employ a deep residual multilayer perceptron comprising 88 layers to accurately model the light field. Crucially, we find that successfully training such a deep NeLF requires ample training data, which we obtain by transferring knowledge from a pretrained NeRF through a data distillation process. Comprehensive evaluation on both synthetic and real datasets demonstrates that our approach surpasses competing methods. Specifically, on synthetic datasets, our method attains a 26 to 35-fold reduction in floating-point operations per camera ray and a 28 to 31-fold improvement in runtime, while also achieving a notable enhancement in rendering fidelity, with an average PSNR gain between 1.4 and 2.8 dB compared to NeRF, all without relying on specialized parallel computing techniques.

author: Farmer
title: Enhancing Efficiency in 3D Object Detection through Knowledge Distillation Techniques
abstract: Advanced 3D object detectors often face significant computational demands despite notable advancements. Addressing this, we investigate knowledge distillation (KD) as a means to develop efficient 3D object detectors, concentrating on widely-used pillar- and voxel-based architectures. Lacking established teacher-student frameworks, we initially analyze strategies for obtaining student networks that balance accuracy and computational cost, considering both model compression and reduced input resolution. Subsequently, we establish a benchmarking framework to evaluate existing KD strategies from 2D contexts applied to 3D object detection, utilizing six rigorously defined teacher-student configurations. Moreover, we introduce a refined KD procedure that leverages an improved logit distillation approach targeting only a select subset of critical locations identified by the teacher's classification response, along with a teacher-directed student initialization method to transfer feature extraction capabilities via weight inheritance. Comprehensive testing on the Waymo dataset demonstrates the top-performing model reaches 65.75% LEVEL 2 mAPH, outperforming the teacher while consuming merely 44% of its floating-point operations. The fastest student model achieves 51 FPS on an NVIDIA A100, outperforming PointPillar by a factor of 2.2 and delivering superior accuracy. The implementation is accessible at https://github.com/CVMI-Lab/SparseKD.

author: Ryan
title: Transferring knowledge from multi-modal to single-modality segmentation models via distillation
abstract: Combining multiple imaging modalities has been extensively explored for medical image segmentation, showing enhanced accuracy compared to single-modality approaches across various tasks. Despite this, clinical constraints such as limited physician availability, scanner access, and cost considerations typically restrict acquisitions to a single modality. In this work, we introduce a framework that distills knowledge from a trained multi-modal segmentation network (teacher) into a mono-modal network (student). This strategy adapts the generalized distillation approach, where the student learns from one modality out of the multiple inputs used by the teacher. We demonstrate the utility of this framework on brain tumor segmentation using the BraTS 2018 dataset. Evaluations across architectures indicate that the student network successfully assimilates the teacher’s knowledge and consistently surpasses the standard mono-modal baseline in segmentation performance.

author: Osborne
title: Transferring Knowledge from Deep Neural Networks Applied to Healthcare Analysis
abstract: The surge in Electronic Healthcare Records (EHR) has generated both challenges and opportunities for computational phenotyping by enabling the extraction of meaningful disease-related data representations. Although deep learning architectures achieve strong predictive accuracy in computational phenotyping, they lack transparency, which is essential for clinical use. We present a new knowledge distillation technique, termed interpretable mimic learning, that aims to replicate deep model predictions while producing phenotype features accessible to human understanding. Our approach employs Gradient Boosting Trees to capture interpretable characteristics derived from deep learning frameworks including Stacked Denoising Autoencoder and Long Short-Term Memory networks. Comprehensive testing on a clinical time-series dataset demonstrates that our proposed method matches or surpasses the deep learning baselines and facilitates phenotype interpretability to support clinical decision processes.

author: Moreno
title: Perception-Integrated High-Speed Navigation for Quadrotors in Dense Obstacle Fields
abstract: In autonomous navigation of quadrotors through dense obstacle settings, recent advances in neural control policies have surpassed traditional model-based planning and control techniques in achieving minimal completion time. Yet, these neural policies lack integration with perception, a critical aspect for vision-dependent navigation given the camera's constrained viewing angle and the quadrotor's underactuated dynamics. We introduce a learning-oriented framework that enables perception-integrated agile flight under cluttered conditions. This framework employs a combination of imitation and reinforcement learning, utilizing a privileged learning-by-cheating paradigm. Initially, reinforcement learning trains a perception-aware teacher policy that has access to complete state information to accomplish minimal-time navigation through obstacles. Subsequently, imitation learning is applied to transfer this expertise to a vision-only student policy relying solely on camera inputs. Our method intimately integrates perception and control mechanisms, resulting in a tenfold increase in computational efficiency alongside improved success rates. The efficacy of the closed-loop control is validated through hardware-in-the-loop simulation experiments.

author: Smith
title: Creating Compact, Efficient, and High-Quality Pretrained Language Models for Specialized Domains via Adaptation and Distillation
abstract: Pretrained large-scale models have demonstrated strong performance across various natural language processing applications. Yet, their application in specialized domains often faces domain shift issues and poses difficulties during fine-tuning and deployment under latency and resource constraints. We introduce a universal framework to produce compact, rapid, and effective pretrained models tailored for particular domains. Our method involves adapting pretrained models designed for general usage by means of task-independent knowledge distillation within the targeted domains. In particular, we introduce domain-specific vocabulary augmentation at the adaptation phase, selecting the incremental vocabulary size automatically based on corpus-level occurrence frequencies. Subsequently, we evaluate multiple compression strategies for large pretrained models customized to domain-specific contexts. Our experiments focus on the biomedical and computer science areas. Results indicate that our technique yields superior outcomes compared to the BERT BASE model on domain-related tasks, while being 3.3 times smaller and 5.1 times faster than BERT BASE. The implementation and pretrained checkpoints can be found at https://aka.ms/adalm.

author: Nguyen
title: Teacher-Student Training for Compact Highway Deep Neural Networks
abstract: Over recent years, deep learning has driven remarkable improvements in speech recognition capabilities. Despite this progress, neural network acoustic models generally possess a much larger size than traditional Gaussian mixture models, limiting their suitability for deployment on embedded systems. Earlier work explored a compact acoustic model based on highway deep neural networks (HDNN), which are feedforward networks incorporating depth-gated connections. Findings demonstrated that HDNN acoustic models maintain recognition performance comparable to standard deep neural networks (DNNs) while reducing model parameters substantially. The current study extends this line of research by applying knowledge distillation, or teacher-student training, where a smaller HDNN is supervised by a more accurate, larger model during training. Additionally, the effects of sequence-level training and model adaptation are examined within this framework. Experimental validation took place using the AMI meeting speech dataset. Results reveal a notable enhancement in recognition accuracy of the sub-0.8 million parameter HDNN model, considerably closing the performance disparity with a standard DNN featuring 30 million parameters.
